questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =16(1) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

questions.problem:
The Cartesian equation of the circle defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -3,\,y=5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4,\,0\le \theta <2\pi 
$$

is given by

$(x\,+$
{{field-1}}$)^{2}+(y\,-$
{{field-2}}$)^{2}=$
{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+3}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ (x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is $(x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=25.$

\begin{aligned}y+3 & =\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{6}{5}(y+3) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{36}{25}{(y+3)}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the circle of radius $2$ centered at the origin, as shown below. Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(2,0).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/156d160267551e9dbf4db42b14b1e0dbb46ab658a836a760cf31a42eb89662d3.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$ centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius is $r = 2.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=2\cos\theta,\quad y=2\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a set of parametric equations, defined for $\theta\in[0,2\pi),$ that generates a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(4,6).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x= r\cos\theta+a,\quad y=r\sin\theta+b,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, the radius $r = 6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/4bd384e2b1a9d0568617ddbfd5ac7dbe9630882b45c40d7912f4809a6e0be551.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right],$ we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$

Example: 
                    Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$

tutorials.name: Converting the Parametric Equations of a Circle to Cartesian Form
tutorials.problem:
To convert the parametric equations of a circle to a Cartesian equation, we can eliminate the parameter $\theta$ using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

To demonstrate, consider the circle defined parametrically as

$$
x=5\cos\theta,\quad y=5\sin\theta, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $x^2+y^2 = 25.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the circle of radius 16 centered at the origin, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(16,0)?

a
x=32cos⁡θ,y=32sin⁡θ
b
x=16sin⁡θ,y=16cos⁡θ
c
x=4cos⁡θ,y=4sin⁡θ
d
x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ
e
x=4sin⁡θ,y=4cos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r,0).

In our case, the radius r=16. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 7 centered at the origin?

a
x=49sin⁡θ,y=49cos⁡θ
b
x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ
c
x=3.5sin⁡θ,y=3,5cos⁡θ
d
x=14sin⁡θ,y=14cos⁡θ
e
x=7sin⁡θ,y=7cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=7. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius is $r=4.$ Substituting $r=4$ gives

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin?

a
x=9sin⁡θ,y=9cos⁡θ
b
x=sin⁡θ+3,y=cos⁡θ+3
c
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
d
x=3sin⁡θ,y=3cos⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=3. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=\frac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

x= r\cos\theta+a,\quad y=r\sin\theta+b,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

For example, the parametric equations of a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(1,-2)$ are

$$
x= 2\cos\theta+1,\quad y=2\sin\theta-2,\quad  \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

These parametric equations traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(3,-2),$ the rightmost point on the curve.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=2sin⁡θ+3
b
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ
c
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
e
x=3cos⁡θ−1,y=3sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-4,5).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +5,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +5,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Consider the circle of radius 3 centered at (−4,5), as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(−1,5)?

a
x=3sin⁡θ+5,y=3cos⁡θ−4
b
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−4
c
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
d
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
e
x=3sin⁡θ−4,y=3cos⁡θ+5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r+a,b).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−4,5). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -6,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -6,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6)?

a
x=4cos⁡θ−6,y=4sin⁡θ+6
b
x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6
c
x=4cos⁡θ+6,y=4sin⁡θ−6
d
x=cos⁡θ+6,y=sin⁡θ−4
e
x=cos⁡θ−4,y=sin⁡θ+6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6,θ∈[0,2π).

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

In our case, the radius $r = 6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta$ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/4bd384e2b1a9d0568617ddbfd5ac7dbe9630882b45c40d7912f4809a6e0be551.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta$ to $\left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right],$ we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=6\cos\theta,\quad y=6\sin\theta, \quad \theta \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis.

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\frac{5\pi }{4}]$, we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\frac{5\pi }{4}].
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations

x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ.

What is the domain of the parameter θ?

a
[0,π]
b
[π2,π]
c
[π2,3π2]
d
[0,π2]
e
[π2,2π)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=2. So, the parametric equations of the full circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter θ with the central angle formed by a point (x,y) on the circle and the x-axis.

We can see that if we restrict θ to [π2,π], we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[π2,π].

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=6.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/37665aa7ea5388a1162ca68a1662aaa86d6369f083d7563dbf27c521c13a7c72.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}]$, we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are 

$$
x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}].
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The arc of a circle above is defined by the parametric equations

x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ.

What is the domain of the parameter θ?

a
θ∈[0,π4]
b
θ∈[0,2π3]
c
θ∈[0,3π4]
d
θ∈[0,π2]
e
θ∈[0,3π2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=3. So, the parametric equations of the full circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter θ with the central angle formed by a point (x,y) on the circle and the x-axis.

We can see that if we restrict θ to [0,3π4], we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,3π4].

tutorial.name: Converting the Parametric Equations of a Circle to Cartesian Form
tutorial.problem:
To convert the parametric equations of a circle to a Cartesian equation, we can eliminate the parameter $\theta$ using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

To demonstrate, consider the circle defined parametrically as

$$
x=5\cos\theta,\quad y=5\sin\theta, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $x^2+y^2 = 25.$

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example:  Parametrizing Part of a Circle
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta.$ We can do this using the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = 1
$$

By isolating the $\cos\theta$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{3} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\sin\theta$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y+4}{3} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{{3}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these values into the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{9}+\frac{(y+4)^{2}}{9} & =1 \\ (x-2)^{2}+(y+4)^{2} & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is $(x-2)^2 + (y+4)^2 = 9.$

question.problem:

x=3\cos\theta + 2,\quad y=3\sin\theta - 4, \quad 0\leq\theta\lt 2\pi.

observed_steps.name: Question 16
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=12cos⁡θ,y=12sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=12
b
x2+y2=12
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=12
e
x2−y2=14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=12cos⁡θx2=(12cos⁡θ)2=14cos2⁡θ.

By squaring the y-equation, we get

y=12sin⁡θy2=(12sin⁡θ)2=14sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=14cos2⁡θ+14sin2⁡θ=14(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=14(1)=14.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=14.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =16(1) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

question.html:
Question 18
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=7
b
x2−y2=56
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=7
e
x2+y2=49
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=7cos⁡θx2=(7cos⁡θ)2=49cos2⁡θ. By squaring the y-equation, we get y=7sin⁡θy2=(7sin⁡θ)2=49sin2⁡θ. Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=49cos2⁡θ+49sin2⁡θ=49(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=49(1)=49. Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=49.

Question 1
?

Consider the circle of radius 16 centered at the origin, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(16,0)?

a
x=32cos⁡θ,y=32sin⁡θ
b
x=16sin⁡θ,y=16cos⁡θ
c
x=4cos⁡θ,y=4sin⁡θ
d
x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ
e
x=4sin⁡θ,y=4cos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r,0).

In our case, the radius r=16. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$ centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius $r=16.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the circle of radius 16 centered at the origin, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(16,0)?

a
x=32cos⁡θ,y=32sin⁡θ
b
x=16sin⁡θ,y=16cos⁡θ
c
x=4cos⁡θ,y=4sin⁡θ
d
x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ
e
x=4sin⁡θ,y=4cos⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r,0).

In our case, the radius r=16. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=16cos⁡θ,y=16sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

solution.reasoning: Option d satisfies x²+y²=256, starts at (16,0) when θ=0, and initially moves upward, so increasing θ traverses the circle counterclockwise exactly once on [0,2π). The supplied example supports this parametrization, but no answer key or grade for the current question is captured.

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r,0).$

In our case, the radius $r=16.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $7$ centered at the origin?
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 7 centered at the origin?

a
x=49sin⁡θ,y=49cos⁡θ
b
x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ
c
x=3.5sin⁡θ,y=3,5cos⁡θ
d
x=14sin⁡θ,y=14cos⁡θ
e
x=7sin⁡θ,y=7cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=7. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $7$ centered at the origin?
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 7 centered at the origin?

a
x=49sin⁡θ,y=49cos⁡θ
b
x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ
c
x=3.5sin⁡θ,y=3,5cos⁡θ
d
x=14sin⁡θ,y=14cos⁡θ
e
x=7sin⁡θ,y=7cos⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=7. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

solution.reasoning: Option b gives x²+y²=49(cos²θ+sin²θ)=49, the circle centered at the origin with radius 7. The interval [0,2π) covers the entire circle. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $7$ centered at the origin?
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=7.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin?
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=3.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin?

a
x=9sin⁡θ,y=9cos⁡θ
b
x=sin⁡θ+3,y=cos⁡θ+3
c
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
d
x=3sin⁡θ,y=3cos⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=3. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin?

a
x=9sin⁡θ,y=9cos⁡θ
b
x=sin⁡θ+3,y=cos⁡θ+3
c
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
d
x=3sin⁡θ,y=3cos⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=3. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

solution.reasoning: Option e gives x²+y²=9(cos²θ+sin²θ)=9, a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin, and [0,2π) covers it completely. No MA answer key or grade for this question is captured.

Question 4
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin?

a
x=9sin⁡θ,y=9cos⁡θ
b
x=sin⁡θ+3,y=cos⁡θ+3
c
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
d
x=3sin⁡θ,y=3cos⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=3. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $\frac{1}{3}$ centered at the origin?
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=\frac{1}{3}.$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are 

$$
x=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 13 centered at the origin?

a
x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ
b
x=23cos⁡θ,y=23sin⁡θ
c
x=19cos⁡θ,y=19sin⁡θ
d
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=13. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 13 centered at the origin?

a
x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ
b
x=23cos⁡θ,y=23sin⁡θ
c
x=19cos⁡θ,y=19sin⁡θ
d
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=13. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

solution.reasoning: Option a gives x²+y²=(1/9)(cos²θ+sin²θ)=1/9, a circle centered at the origin with radius 1/3. The interval [0,2π) covers the entire circle. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

x=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).

Question 5
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 13 centered at the origin?

a
x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ
b
x=23cos⁡θ,y=23sin⁡θ
c
x=19cos⁡θ,y=19sin⁡θ
d
x=9cos⁡θ,y=9sin⁡θ
e
x=3cos⁡θ,y=3sin⁡θ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=13. Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=13cos⁡θ,y=13sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at the Origin

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(-5,-2)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $2$ centered at the point $(-5,-2).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -5,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -2,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
b
 x=2cos⁡θ+2,y=2sin⁡θ+5
c
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
d
x=cos⁡θ−5,y=sin⁡θ−2
e
x=2cos⁡θ+5,y=2sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2,θ∈[0,2π).

last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
b
 x=2cos⁡θ+2,y=2sin⁡θ+5
c
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
d
x=cos⁡θ−5,y=sin⁡θ−2
e
x=2cos⁡θ+5,y=2sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2,θ∈[0,2π).

solution.reasoning: Option a satisfies (x+5)²+(y+2)²=4(cos²θ+sin²θ)=4, giving a circle of radius 2 centered at (-5,-2). The interval [0,2π) covers the entire circle. No MA answer key or grade for the current question is captured.

Question 6
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
b
 x=2cos⁡θ+2,y=2sin⁡θ+5
c
x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2
d
x=cos⁡θ−5,y=sin⁡θ−2
e
x=2cos⁡θ+5,y=2sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 2 centered at the point (−5,−2). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=2cos⁡θ−5,y=2sin⁡θ−2,θ∈[0,2π).

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-2,3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-2,3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=2sin⁡θ+3
b
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ
c
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
e
x=3cos⁡θ−1,y=3sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3,θ∈[0,2π).

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=2sin⁡θ+3
b
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ
c
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
e
x=3cos⁡θ−1,y=3sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

solution.reasoning: Option c satisfies (x+2)²+(y−3)²=9(cos²θ+sin²θ)=9, so it generates the circle of radius 3 centered at (-2,3). The interval [0,2π) covers the whole circle. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-2,3)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-2,3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -2,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3)?

a
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=2sin⁡θ+3
b
x=2cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ
c
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3
e
x=3cos⁡θ−1,y=3sin⁡θ+2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−2,3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ−2,y=3sin⁡θ+3,θ∈[0,2π).

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/6b77b1b8a61b5ec7306fbc0b3d70618e7fdce2237bdcbfd017c23c01b80f2979.png)

Consider the circle of radius $3$ centered at $(-4,5)$, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(-1,5)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-4,5).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +5,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the circle of radius 3 centered at (−4,5), as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(−1,5)?

a
x=3sin⁡θ+5,y=3cos⁡θ−4
b
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−4
c
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
d
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
e
x=3sin⁡θ−4,y=3cos⁡θ+5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r+a,b).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−4,5). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5,θ∈[0,2π).

The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +5,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Consider the circle of radius 3 centered at (−4,5), as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(−1,5)?

a
x=3sin⁡θ+5,y=3cos⁡θ−4
b
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−4
c
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
d
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
e
x=3sin⁡θ−4,y=3cos⁡θ+5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r+a,b).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−4,5). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

solution.reasoning: Option d satisfies (x+4)²+(y−5)²=9 and starts at (-1,5) when θ=0. Its initial velocity is (0,3), so it moves counterclockwise and traverses the circle once over [0,2π). No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

Consider the circle of radius $3$ centered at $(-4,5)$, as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$  traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point $A(-1,5)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from $(r+a,b).$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(-4,5).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -4,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +5,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

feedback.html:
Question 8
?

Consider the circle of radius 3 centered at (−4,5), as shown above. Which of the following sets of parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), traverse the circle once in the counterclockwise direction starting at the point A(−1,5)?

a
x=3sin⁡θ+5,y=3cos⁡θ−4
b
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−4
c
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
d
x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5
e
x=3sin⁡θ−4,y=3cos⁡θ+5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

Under this parametrization, the circle is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, starting from (r+a,b).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (−4,5). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are x=3cos⁡θ−4,y=3sin⁡θ+5,θ∈[0,2π).

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -6,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6)?

a
x=4cos⁡θ−6,y=4sin⁡θ+6
b
x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6
c
x=4cos⁡θ+6,y=4sin⁡θ−6
d
x=cos⁡θ+6,y=sin⁡θ−4
e
x=cos⁡θ−4,y=sin⁡θ+6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6,θ∈[0,2π).

last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -6,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6)?

a
x=4cos⁡θ−6,y=4sin⁡θ+6
b
x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6
c
x=4cos⁡θ+6,y=4sin⁡θ−6
d
x=cos⁡θ+6,y=sin⁡θ−4
e
x=cos⁡θ−4,y=sin⁡θ+6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

solution.reasoning: Option b satisfies (x−4)²+(y+6)²=cos²θ+sin²θ=1, giving the circle of radius 1 centered at (4,-6). The interval [0,2π) covers the entire circle. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $1$ centered at the point $(4,-6).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -6,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6)?

a
x=4cos⁡θ−6,y=4sin⁡θ+6
b
x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6
c
x=4cos⁡θ+6,y=4sin⁡θ−6
d
x=cos⁡θ+6,y=sin⁡θ−4
e
x=cos⁡θ−4,y=sin⁡θ+6
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 1 centered at the point (4,−6). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=cos⁡θ+4,y=sin⁡θ−6,θ∈[0,2π).

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3)?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (5,−3)?

a
x=3cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ+5
b
x=9cos⁡θ+5,y=9sin⁡θ−3
c
x=3cos⁡θ−5,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ+3,y=3sin⁡θ−5
e
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (5,−3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−3,θ∈[0,2π).
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Circle Centered at a General Point

solution.reasoning: Option e satisfies (x−5)²+(y+3)²=9(cos²θ+sin²θ)=9, giving a circle of radius 3 centered at (5,-3). The interval [0,2π) covers the entire circle. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 10
feedback.problem: Which of the following parametric equations, defined for $\theta \in [0,2\pi ),$ generate a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle of radius $r$ centered at the point $(a,b)$ are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +a,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +b,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, we have a circle of radius $3$ centered at the point $(5,-3).$ Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +5,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -3,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following parametric equations, defined for θ∈[0,2π), generate a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (5,−3)?

a
x=3cos⁡θ−3,y=3sin⁡θ+5
b
x=9cos⁡θ+5,y=9sin⁡θ−3
c
x=3cos⁡θ−5,y=3sin⁡θ+3
d
x=3cos⁡θ+3,y=3sin⁡θ−5
e
x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the point (a,b) are x=rcos⁡θ+a,y=rsin⁡θ+b,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, we have a circle of radius 3 centered at the point (5,−3). Therefore, the parametric equations of the circle are

x=3cos⁡θ+5,y=3sin⁡θ−3,θ∈[0,2π).

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/a0ec11769fa20feb317ef502f41e1d31ffe539d4b17a51ad46b8487c17752021.png)

The arc of a circle above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $\theta ?$
question.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=2.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/9752e135eee9c4e585a007f84b0b8b8d220d4e2e1f027fc8a69aebf27066940e.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\frac{5\pi }{4}]$, we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\frac{5\pi }{4}].
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example:  Parametrizing Part of a Circle
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=2.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/9752e135eee9c4e585a007f84b0b8b8d220d4e2e1f027fc8a69aebf27066940e.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\frac{5\pi }{4}]$, we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\frac{5\pi }{4}].
$$

Question 11
?

The arc of a circle above is defined by the parametric equations

x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ.

What is the domain of the parameter θ?

a
θ∈[0,π4]
b
θ∈[0,3π4]
c
θ∈[0,3π2]
d
θ∈[0,5π2]
e
θ∈[0,5π4]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=2. So, the parametric equations of the full circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter θ with the central angle formed by a point (x,y) on the circle and the x-axis.

We can see that if we restrict θ to [0,5π4], we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,5π4].

solution.reasoning: The depicted arc runs counterclockwise from the positive x-axis through the upper semicircle to the lower-left endpoint at angle 5π/4. Both endpoints are included, so option e gives the domain [0,5π/4]. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

question.html:
Question 13
?

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations

x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ.

What is the domain of the parameter θ?

a
[0,π]
b
[π2,π]
c
[π2,3π2]
d
[0,π2]
e
[π2,2π)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=2. So, the parametric equations of the full circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter θ with the central angle formed by a point (x,y) on the circle and the x-axis.

We can see that if we restrict θ to [π2,π], we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[π2,π].

last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=2.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/b76043921a3f9399049d6c3b4f557c7263da4d38a070c66a2dd444dbe2806c8e.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]$, we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ].
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

The quarter-circle above is defined by the parametric equations

x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ.

What is the domain of the parameter θ?

a
[0,π]
b
[π2,π]
c
[π2,3π2]
d
[0,π2]
e
[π2,2π)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The parametric equations of a circle of radius r centered at the origin are

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

In our case, the radius r=2. So, the parametric equations of the full circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[0,2π).

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter θ with the central angle formed by a point (x,y) on the circle and the x-axis.

We can see that if we restrict θ to [π2,π], we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are x=2cos⁡θ,y=2sin⁡θ,θ∈[π2,π].

$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=2.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-circle, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/b76043921a3f9399049d6c3b4f557c7263da4d38a070c66a2dd444dbe2806c8e.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]$, we get the required quarter-circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the quarter-circle are 

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ].
$$

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example:  Parametrizing Part of a Circle
last_observation.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a circle  of radius $r$  centered at  the origin are

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

In our case, the radius $r=3.$ So, the parametric equations of the *full* circle are 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

To restrict the parameterization to the arc above, we associate the parameter $\theta $ with the central angle formed by a point $(x,y)$ on the circle and the $x$-axis. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221931/assets/5cc99d78c5fe5afacde4ba96e2a4010b0fab66bdabbe5c2b518bd936f36c7d84.png)

We can see that if we restrict $\theta $ to $[0,\frac{3\pi }{4}]$, we get the required arc of the circle.

Therefore, the parametric equations of the arc of the circle are 

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\theta \in [0,\frac{3\pi }{4}].
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=12cos⁡θ,y=12sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=12
b
x2+y2=12
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=12
e
x2−y2=14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=12cos⁡θx2=(12cos⁡θ)2=14cos2⁡θ.

By squaring the y-equation, we get

y=12sin⁡θy2=(12sin⁡θ)2=14sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=14cos2⁡θ+14sin2⁡θ=14(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=14(1)=14.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=14.

last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=12cos⁡θ,y=12sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=12
b
x2+y2=12
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=12
e
x2−y2=14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=12cos⁡θx2=(12cos⁡θ)2=14cos2⁡θ.

By squaring the y-equation, we get

y=12sin⁡θy2=(12sin⁡θ)2=14sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=14cos2⁡θ+14sin2⁡θ=14(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=14(1)=14.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=14.

feedback.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.$

feedback.html:
Question 16
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=12cos⁡θ,y=12sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=12
b
x2+y2=12
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=12
e
x2−y2=14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=12cos⁡θx2=(12cos⁡θ)2=14cos2⁡θ.

By squaring the y-equation, we get

y=12sin⁡θy2=(12sin⁡θ)2=14sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=14cos2⁡θ+14sin2⁡θ=14(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=14(1)=14.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=14.

question.name: Question 17
question.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =16(1) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Parametrized Circle
last_observation.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +16{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =16(1) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$

question.html:
Question 17
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=4cos⁡θ,y=4sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=8
b
x2−y2=16
c
x2+y2=4
d
x2−y2=2
e
x2+y2=16
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=4cos⁡θx2=(4cos⁡θ)2=16cos2⁡θ, By squaring the y-equation, we get y=4sin⁡θy2=(4sin⁡θ)2=16sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=16cos2⁡θ+16sin2⁡θ=16(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=16(1)=16.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=16.

solution.reasoning: Squaring and adding eliminates θ: x²+y²=16(cos²θ+sin²θ)=16. Thus option e is correct mathematically. No current-question MA answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.html:
Question 17
?

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=4cos⁡θ,y=4sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=8
b
x2−y2=16
c
x2+y2=4
d
x2−y2=2
e
x2+y2=16
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=4cos⁡θx2=(4cos⁡θ)2=16cos2⁡θ, By squaring the y-equation, we get y=4sin⁡θy2=(4sin⁡θ)2=16sin2⁡θ.

Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=16cos2⁡θ+16sin2⁡θ=16(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=16(1)=16.

Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=16.

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

$$
x=7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi .
$$
question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the $x$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ {x}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By squaring the $y$-equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ {y}^{2} & =(7\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =49{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +49{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =49({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =49(1) \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49.$

Question 18

Calculate the Cartesian equation of the circle

x=7cos⁡θ,y=7sin⁡θ,0≤θ<2π.

a
x2+y2=7
b
x2−y2=56
c
x2+y2=14
d
x2−y2=7
e
x2+y2=49
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter θ. We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By squaring the x-equation, we get x=7cos⁡θx2=(7cos⁡θ)2=49cos2⁡θ. By squaring the y-equation, we get y=7sin⁡θy2=(7sin⁡θ)2=49sin2⁡θ. Adding the two equations and using cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ=1, we get x2+y2=49cos2⁡θ+49sin2⁡θ=49(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=49(1)=49. Therefore the Cartesian equation is x2+y2=49.

question.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+3}{5} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-4}{5} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{(x+3)^{2}}{25}+\frac{(y-4)^{2}}{25} & =1 \\ (x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian equation is $(x+3)^{2}+(y-4)^{2}=25.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$

If $y=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(2x-1),$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(2x-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2x-1)^{2}-1}}\cdot (2x-1)^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(4{x}^{2}-4x+1)-1}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-4x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4x(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x-1)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

If $y=4\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(3x-4),$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(4\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(3x-4)) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(3x-4)) \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{(3x-4)^{2}-1}}\cdot (3x-4)^{′} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{(3x-4)^{2}-1}}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{12}{\sqrt{(3x-4)^{2}-1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$

If $y=-\sqrt{7}\,\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\sqrt{3}\,x),$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
{{field-1}}

$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic tangent function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{artanh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\sqrt{7}\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\sqrt{3}\,x)) \\  & =-\sqrt{7}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{artanh}⁡(\sqrt{3}\,x)) \\  & =-\sqrt{7}\cdot \frac{1}{1-{(\sqrt{3}\,x)}^{2}}\cdot {(\sqrt{3}\,x)}^{′} \\  & =-\sqrt{7}\cdot \frac{1}{1-3{x}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{21}}{3{x}^{2}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$
