questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$

Calculate ${g}^{′}(x)$ for $g(x)={e}^{x}\,\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3).$

| $\text{d}y$ | $={e}^{x}\,\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3)\,+$ | $4{e}^{x}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\text{d}x$ |  | {{field-1}} |
questions.worked_solution:
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic sine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arsinh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}}.
$$

 

And the product rule is

$$
\frac{\text{d}(u\cdot v)}{\text{d}x}={u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)+u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)
$$

Using the product rule, chain rule, and  formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & ={({e}^{x})}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3)+{e}^{x}\cdot {(\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3))}^{′} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot \operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3)+{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4x+3)^{2}+1}}\cdot {(4x+3)}^{′} \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot \operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3)+{e}^{x}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{(4x+3)^{2}+1}}\cdot 4 \\  & ={e}^{x}\,\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(4x+3)+\frac{4{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{(4x+3)^{2}+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If y=arcosh⁡(2x−1), then dydx=

a
2x(x−1)
b
2x(2x−1)
c
1x(x−2)
d
1x(x−1)
e
1x(2x−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is ddx(arcosh⁡x)=1x2−1.

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

dydx=ddx(arcosh⁡(2x−1))=1(2x−1)2−1⋅(2x−1)′=1(4x2−4x+1)−1⋅2=24x2−4x=24x(x−1)=1x(x−1).

question.problem:
$$

If $y=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(2x-1),$ then $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=$
question.worked_solution:
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-1}}.
$$

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(2x-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2x-1)^{2}-1}}\cdot (2x-1)^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(4{x}^{2}-4x+1)-1}}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}-4x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{4x(x-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x-1)}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If y=arcosh⁡(2x−1), then dydx=

a
2x(x−1)
b
2x(2x−1)
c
1x(x−2)
d
1x(x−1)
e
1x(2x−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is ddx(arcosh⁡x)=1x2−1.

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

dydx=ddx(arcosh⁡(2x−1))=1(2x−1)2−1⋅(2x−1)′=1(4x2−4x+1)−1⋅2=24x2−4x=24x(x−1)=1x(x−1).

Question 1

If y=arcosh⁡(2x−1), then dydx=

a
2x(x−1)
b
2x(2x−1)
c
1x(x−2)
d
1x(x−1)
e
1x(2x−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The formula for the derivative of the inverse hyperbolic cosine function is ddx(arcosh⁡x)=1x2−1.

Using the formula above with the chain rule, we get

dydx=ddx(arcosh⁡(2x−1))=1(2x−1)2−1⋅(2x−1)′=1(4x2−4x+1)−1⋅2=24x2−4x=24x(x−1)=1x(x−1).

solution.reasoning: The chain rule gives dy/dx = 2/\sqrt{(2x-1)^2-1} = 2/\sqrt{4x(x-1)} = 1/\sqrt{x(x-1)} for x>1, so option d is correct. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence is provided.

questions.problem:
In **ascending order**, the roots of $f(t)=\frac{{t}^{2}-4t-21}{{t}^{2}+7t+10}$ are

questions.worked_solution:
The roots of $f(t)$ are the solutions to the equation $f(t)=0.$ In our case, we have

$$
\frac{{t}^{2}-4t-21}{{t}^{2}+7t+10}=0.
$$

First, we factor $f(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\frac{{t}^{2}-4t-21}{{t}^{2}+7t+10} \\  & =\frac{(t-7)(t+3)}{(t+5)(t+2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the numerator equal to zero and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(t-7)(t+3) & =0 \\ t & =7,\,-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions to $f(t)=0$, in ascending order, are $t=-3$ and $t=7.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}{2} & =1 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)} & ={7}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}=x+1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={7}^{2} \\ x+1 & =49 \\ x & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find $x$ such that ${log}_{4}⁡(3x-2)=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $4,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{4}⁡(3x-2) & =3 \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(3x-2)} & ={4}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${4}^{{log}_{4}⁡(3x-2)}=3x-2.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2 & ={4}^{3} \\ 3x-2 & =64 \\ 3x & =66 \\ x & =22.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-16{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =-48 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =\frac{-48}{-16} \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)} & ={7}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)}=x-128.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x-128 & ={7}^{3} \\ x-128 & =343 \\ x & =471.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}{2} & =1 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x+1) & =2 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)} & ={7}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x+1)}=x+1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & ={7}^{2} \\ x+1 & =49 \\ x & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

log7⁡(x+1)2=1log7⁡(x+1)=2

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is 7, so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

log7⁡(x+1)=27log7⁡(x+1)=72

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get 7log7⁡(x+1)=x+1.

Therefore, x+1=72x+1=49x=48.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange our equation to isolate the logarithmic term:

$$
\begin{aligned}-16{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =-48 \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =\frac{-48}{-16} \\ {log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the logarithm, we exponentiate both sides of the equation. The base of the logarithm is $7,$ so we use this base for the exponentiation as well:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{7}⁡(x-128) & =3 \\ {7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)} & ={7}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since exponentiation is the inverse function of the logarithm, we get ${7}^{{log}_{7}⁡(x-128)}=x-128.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}x-128 & ={7}^{3} \\ x-128 & =343 \\ x & =471.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,i+j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=(t-2)\,i+({t}^{3}-t)\,j$ for $t\in [1,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{3}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}\cdot (1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{2},\pi ]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }25{cos}^{2}⁡t-25{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }25\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{e}^{2t}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+yz\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=t\,i+5t\,j+\,k$ for $t\in [2,3]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=5t,\,z(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =\,i+5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+yz\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{2}^{3}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}\cdot (1)+5t\cdot (5)+1\cdot (0)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}+25t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{t}^{2}\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{3\pi }{2}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{t}^{4}\cdot (2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,dx+\frac{y}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,dx+\frac{y}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}-0]-[0-4] \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}x\,dx-z\,dy+y\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the curve $r(t)=3{t}^{2}\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3{t}^{2},\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =6t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{t}^{2}\cdot (6t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9\,dt \\  & =(\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}-9t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =72{\pi }^{4}-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(t)={t}^{2},\,y(t)=4t-1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-1)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+4\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3x+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{2}+4t-1)\cdot 2t+{t}^{2}\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+8{t}^{2}-2t+4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+12{t}^{2}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}(2)^{4}+4(2)^{3}-{2}^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[24+32-4] \\  & =52\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{y}{x}\,dy+dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\pi ].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-\frac{1}{y}\,dx+\frac{y}{x}\,dy+dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{y}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{y}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =(2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =(2\pi -\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =2(\pi +1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy-z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix parametrized by $r(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2t\,k$ for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=2t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy-z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-2t\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t-4t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9-4t\,dt \\  & =(9t-2{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(9-\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$

Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C y\,\mathrm{d}x -x\,\mathrm{d}y ,$ where $C$ is a portion of the ellipse parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t)=\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 3\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in[0,\pi].$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ often come in pairs. For example, 

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

We usually express a sum of line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y$ as a single integral. In the case above, we can write this sum as

$$
\int\limits_C (x+y) \, \textrm dx + (x-y) \, \textrm dy.
$$

Let's evaluate this integral in this case where $C$ is given by the line segment

$$
\mathbf{r}(t)=\underbrace{(6t+1)}_{x(t)} \,\mathbf{i} + \underbrace{(2t+1)}_{y(t)} \,\mathbf{j}, \qquad t\in\left[0,1\right].
$$

Along the path $C,$ we have

$$
x = 6t+1, \qquad y = 2t+1.
$$

Computing the derivative of $\mathbf r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)\,j \\  & =6\,i+2\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate the line integral by applying a change of variables, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}x+(x-y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(6t+1+2t+1)\cdot 6+(6t+1-(2t+1))\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\cdot 6+(4t)\cdot 2\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}48t+12+8t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}56t+12\,\text{d}t \\  & ={28{t}^{2}+12t|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =28+12 \\  & =40.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
tutorials.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function of three variables and $C$ be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy +  \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz
$$

For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:  

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy +   f \, \textrm dz
$$

As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

$$
\int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} +   f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

$$
\int_a^b f x'+ f y' +   f z' \,\textrm d t,
$$

where the primes denote differentiation with respect to $t.$

Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad
y(t) = t^2.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(({x}^{2}+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{t}^{2}+2{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x^2+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + x\,\mathrm{d}y,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $\mathbf{r}(t) = t\,\mathbf{i} + t^2\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in\left[0,1\right].$
question.worked_solution:

$$
x(t) = t, \qquad

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx+1xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=1ti+tj for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫13t−1tdt
b
∫132tdt
c
2∫131tdt
d
∫13t2−1tdt
e
∫13t2+1tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1t,y(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1t)i+ddt(t)j=−1t2i+j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxy2dx+1xdy=∫13xy2dxdtdt+1xdydtdt=∫13(xy2dxdt+1xdydt)dt=∫131t⋅t2⋅(−1t2)+1(1t)⋅1dt=∫13−1t+tdt=∫13t2−1tdt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,i+j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=sin⁡(2t)i+j for t∈[0,2π]?

a
∫02π2sin⁡(4t)dt
b
∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
c
∫02πsin2⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)−1dt
d
∫02πsin⁡(4t)−cos2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫02πsin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=sin⁡(2t),y(t)=1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(sin⁡(2t))i+ddt(1)j=2cos⁡(2t)i.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy=∫02πxdxdtdt+(x2−y2)dydtdt=∫02π(xdxdt+(x2−y2)dydt)dt=∫02πsin⁡(2t)⋅2cos⁡(2t)+(sin2⁡(2t)−12)⋅0dt=∫02π2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)dt=∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$ for $t\in [0,\pi ]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cydx+xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=cos⁡ti+sin⁡tj for t∈[0,π]?

a
∫0πcos⁡tdt
b
∫0πcos⁡t−sin⁡tdt
c
∫0πcos⁡(2t)dt
d
∫0πdt
e
2∫0πcos⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=cos⁡t,y(t)=sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cydx+xdy=∫0πydxdtdt+xdydtdt=∫0π(xdxdt+ydydt)dt=∫0πsin⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+cos⁡t⋅cos⁡tdt=∫0π−sin2⁡t+cos2⁡tdt=∫0πcos⁡(2t)dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-t)\,j \\  & =i+(3{t}^{2}-1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x+2)\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}((x+y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x+2)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(t-2+{t}^{3}-t)\cdot 1+(t-2+2)\cdot (3{t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{3}-2+3{t}^{3}-t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4{t}^{3}-t-2\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4

question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t-2,\,y(t)={t}^{3}-t.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=(t−2)i+(t3−t)j for t∈[1,2]?

a
∫12t(4t2−1)dt
b
∫124t3−t−2dt
c
∫124t3+t−2dt
d
∫124t3−3t−2dt
e
∫124t3−2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t−2,y(t)=t3−t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(t−2)i+ddt(t3−t)j=i+(3t2−1)j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x+y)dx+(x+2)dy=∫12(x+y)dxdtdt+(x+2)dydtdt=∫12((x+y)dxdt+(x+2)dydt)dt=∫12(t−2+t3−t)⋅1+(t−2+2)⋅(3t2−1)dt=∫12t3−2+3t3−tdt=∫124t3−t−2dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x-y)\,dx+(y-x)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}((x-y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(y-x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=2sin⁡ti−2cos⁡tj for t∈[0,π2]?

a
4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
b
2∫0π/2dt
c
2∫0π/22cos⁡(2t)−sin⁡(2t)dt
d
4∫0π/2dt
e
2∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2sin⁡t,y(t)=−2cos⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2sin⁡t)i+ddt(−2cos⁡t)j=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C(x−y)dx+(y−x)dy=∫0π/2(x−y)dxdtdt+(y−x)dydtdt=∫0π/2((x−y)dxdt+(y−x)dydt)dt=∫0π/2(2sin⁡t−(−2cos⁡t))⋅2cos⁡t+(−2cos⁡t−2sin⁡t)⋅2sin⁡tdt=∫0π/24sin⁡tcos⁡t+4cos2⁡t−4cos⁡tsin⁡t−4sin2⁡tdt=∫0π/24(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)dt=∫0π/24cos⁡(2t)dt=4∫0π/2cos⁡(2t)dt

tutorial.name: Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
tutorial.problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function of three variables and $C$ be a path in three-dimensional space. Suppose we want to calculate the following sum of line integrals:

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dy +  \int\limits_C f \, \textrm dz
$$

For notational simplicity, we can express this as a single integral, as follows:  

$$
\int\limits_C f \, \textrm dx + f \, \textrm dy +   f \, \textrm dz
$$

As before, we can evaluate this integral by parameterizing the curve $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then rewriting the integral using a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f\,\text{d}x+f\,\text{d}y+f\,\text{d}z & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+f\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we often omit the large parentheses and simply write

$$
\int_a^b f\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} + f \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d t} +   f \dfrac{\textrm d z}{\textrm d t} \,\textrm d t.
$$

Finally, it can be helpful to switch to prime notation for the derivatives when dealing with complex integrands. In this case, the above formula becomes

$$
\int_a^b f x'+ f y' +   f z' \,\textrm d t,
$$

where the primes denote differentiation with respect to $t.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
question.problem: Construct a definite integral that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^3\,\mathrm{d}x + z\,\mathrm{d}y + y\,\mathrm{d}z,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $\mathbf{r}(t)=2t\,\mathbf{i} + \cos t\,\mathbf{j} + \sin t\,\mathbf{k}$ for $t\in[0,\pi]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) =2t, \qquad 
y(t) = \cos t , \qquad 
z(t) = \sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =2\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2t)^{3}\cdot (2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }16{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the helix $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{\pi }{3}]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}t+2\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C−ydx+xdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=2cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj+tk for t∈[π4,π3]?

a
∫π/4π/3t2−sin⁡tdt
b
∫π/4π/3t2+9dt
c
∫π/4π/3t2+cos2⁡tdt
d
∫π/4π/3t+2dt
e
∫π/4π/3t+2cos⁡2tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2cos⁡t,y(t)=2sin⁡t,z(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j+ddt(t)k=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj+k.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C−ydx+xdy+zdz=∫π/4π/3−ydxdtdt+xdydtdt+zdzdtdt=∫π/4π/3(−ydxdt+xdydt+zdzdt)dt=∫π/4π/3−2sin⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)+2cos⁡t⋅(2cos⁡t)+t⋅1dt=∫π/4π/3t+2sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡tdt=∫π/4π/3t+2dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,z(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{3}\,dx+z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }({x}^{3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}\cdot (1)+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{t}^{3}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cx3dx+zdy+ydz, where C is a portion of the helix r(t)=ti+cos⁡tj+sin⁡tk for t∈[0,π]?

a
∫0πcos3⁡tdt
b
∫0πt3+cos⁡2tdt
c
∫0πcos2⁡t+1dt
d
∫0πt2−cos⁡tdt
e
∫0πcos⁡2t+sin⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t,y(t)=cos⁡t,z(t)=sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(t)i+ddt(cos⁡t)j+ddt(sin⁡t)k=i−sin⁡tj+cos⁡tk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cx3dx+zdy+ydz=∫0πx3dxdtdt+zdydtdt+ydzdtdt=∫0π(x3dxdt+zdydt+ydzdt)dt=∫0πt3⋅(1)+sin⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+cos⁡t⋅(cos⁡t)dt=∫0πt3+cos2⁡t−sin2⁡tdt=∫0πt3+cos⁡2tdt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=5\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)={e}^{t}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }25{cos}^{2}⁡t-25{sin}^{2}⁡t+{e}^{2t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }25\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{e}^{2t}\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cydx+xdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=5cos⁡ti+5sin⁡tj+etk for t∈[π2,π]?

a
∫π/2π5sin⁡2t+e2tdt
b
∫π/2π25sin⁡2t+etdt
c
∫π/2π25cos⁡2t+e2tdt
d
∫π/2π5cos⁡t+e2tdt
e
∫π/2π5cos⁡2t+etdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=5cos⁡t,y(t)=5sin⁡t,z(t)=et.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(5cos⁡t)i+ddt(5sin⁡t)j+ddt(et)k=−5sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj+etk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cydx+xdy+zdz=∫π/2πydxdtdt+xdydtdt+zdzdtdt=∫π/2π(ydxdt+xdydt+zdzdt)dt=∫π/2π5sin⁡t⋅(−5sin⁡t)+5cos⁡t⋅(5cos⁡t)+et⋅etdt=∫π/2π25cos2⁡t−25sin2⁡t+e2tdt=∫π/2π25cos⁡2t+e2tdt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=5t,\,z(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =\,i+5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+yz\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{2}^{3}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}\cdot (1)+5t\cdot (5)+1\cdot (0)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}+25t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}xy\,dx+yz\,dy+z\,dz,$ where $C$ is a portion of the line $r(t)=t\,i+5t\,j+\,k$ for $t\in [2,3]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=t,\,y(t)=5t,\,z(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,k \\  & =\,i+5\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,dx+yz\,dy+z\,dz & ={\int }_{2}^{3}xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}(xy\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+yz\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}\cdot (1)+5t\cdot (5)+1\cdot (0)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}5{t}^{2}+25t\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxydx+yzdy+zdz, where C is a portion of the line r(t)=ti+5tj+k for t∈[2,3]?

a
∫23t3+20tdt
b
∫233t2+13dt
c
∫235t2+25tdt
d
∫23t+12dt
e
∫23t4−4dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=t,y(t)=5t,z(t)=1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(t)i+ddt(5t)j+ddt(1)k=i+5j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxydx+yzdy+zdz=∫23xydxdtdt+yzdydtdt+zdzdtdt=∫23(xydxdt+yzdydt+zdzdt)dt=∫235t2⋅(1)+5t⋅(5)+1⋅(0)dt=∫235t2+25tdt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)={t}^{2}.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,k \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy+{z}^{2}\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+{z}^{2}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+{t}^{4}\cdot (2t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}2{t}^{5}-4\,dt\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10

$$

$$

$$

question.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C−ydx+xdy+z2dz, where C is a portion of the curve r(t)=2cos⁡ti−2sin⁡tj+t2k for t∈[0,3π2]?

a
∫03π/22t3+2dt
b
∫03π/22t4−2sin2⁡tdt
c
∫03π/22t3+sin2⁡tdt
d
∫03π/22t5−4dt
e
∫03π/22t4−2cos⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=2cos⁡t,y(t)=−2sin⁡t,z(t)=t2.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj+dzdtk=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(−2sin⁡t)j+ddt(t2)k=−2sin⁡ti−2cos⁡tj+2tk.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫C−ydx+xdy+z2dz=∫03π/2−ydxdtdt+xdydtdt+z2dzdtdt=∫03π/2(−ydxdt+xdydt+z2dzdt)dt=∫03π/22sin⁡t⋅(−2sin⁡t)+2cos⁡t⋅(−2cos⁡t)+t4⋅(2t)dt=∫03π/22t5−4sin2⁡t−4cos2⁡tdt=∫03π/22t5−4dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z

observed_steps.name: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X, Y, and Z
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t) = \cos t, \qquad
y(t) = 3\sin t.
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(y\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }-3{sin}^{2}⁡t-3{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & =-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\,dt \\  & =-3{t|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-3\pi \end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,dx+\frac{y}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{x}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{y}{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t-4\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[-\frac{1}{2}-0]-[0-4] \\  & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate ∫Cxydx+yxdy, where C is a portion of the ellipse r(t)=cos⁡ti+2sin⁡tj for t∈[0,π2].

a
72
b
2
c
−12
d
54
e
4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=cos⁡t,y(t)=2sin⁡t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj.

We can now evaluate the line integral:

∫Cxydx+yxdy=∫0π/2xy⋅dxdtdt+yx⋅dydtdt=∫0π/2(xy⋅dxdt+yx⋅dydt)dt=∫0π/2cos⁡t2sin⁡t⋅(−sin⁡t)+2sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅(2cos⁡t)dt=∫0π/2−12cos⁡t+4sin⁡tdt=−12sin⁡t−4cos⁡t|0π/2=[−12−0]−[0−4]=72
question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating a Line Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3{t}^{2},\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =6t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-z\,dy+y\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{t}^{2}\cdot (6t)-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9{cos}^{2}⁡t-9{sin}^{2}⁡t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }18{t}^{3}-9\,dt \\  & =(\frac{9{t}^{4}}{2}-9t){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =72{\pi }^{4}-18\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Along the curve, we have

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3x+y)\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}((3x+y)\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{t}^{2}+4t-1)\cdot 2t+{t}^{2}\cdot 4\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+8{t}^{2}-2t+4{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6{t}^{3}+12{t}^{2}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{3}{2}(2)^{4}+4(2)^{3}-{2}^{2}]-[0] \\  & =[24+32-4] \\  & =52\end{aligned}

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,z(t)=2t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,k \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}-y\,dx+x\,dy-z\,dz & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-2t\cdot 2\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t-4t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9-4t\,dt \\  & =(9t-2{t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(9-\pi )\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx+1xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=1ti+tj for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫13t−1tdt
b
∫132tdt
c
2∫131tdt
d
∫13t2−1tdt
e
∫13t2+1tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1t,y(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1t)i+ddt(t)j=−1t2i+j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxy2dx+1xdy=∫13xy2dxdtdt+1xdydtdt=∫13(xy2dxdt+1xdydt)dt=∫131t⋅t2⋅(−1t2)+1(1t)⋅1dt=∫13−1t+tdt=∫13t2−1tdt

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
last_observation.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxy2dx+1xdy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=1ti+tj for t∈[1,3]?

a
∫13t−1tdt
b
∫132tdt
c
2∫131tdt
d
∫13t2−1tdt
e
∫13t2+1tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=1t,y(t)=t.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(1t)i+ddt(t)j=−1t2i+j.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxy2dx+1xdy=∫13xy2dxdtdt+1xdydtdt=∫13(xy2dxdt+1xdydt)dt=∫131t⋅t2⋅(−1t2)+1(1t)⋅1dt=∫13−1t+tdt=∫13t2−1tdt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

solution.reasoning: With x=1/t and y=t, dx=-dt/t² and dy=dt. Thus xy² dx+(1/x)dy=(-1/t+t)dt=((t²-1)/t)dt, giving option d. The mathematics is conclusive, but no Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\frac{1}{t}\,i+t\,j$ for $t\in [1,3]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\frac{1}{t},\,y(t)=t.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+\frac{1}{x}\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{3}x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(x{y}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{1}{x}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{t}\cdot {t}^{2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{t})}\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}-\frac{1}{t}+t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{{t}^{2}-1}{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,i+j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
question.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=sin⁡(2t)i+j for t∈[0,2π]?

a
∫02π2sin⁡(4t)dt
b
∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
c
∫02πsin2⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)−1dt
d
∫02πsin⁡(4t)−cos2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫02πsin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=sin⁡(2t),y(t)=1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(sin⁡(2t))i+ddt(1)j=2cos⁡(2t)i.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy=∫02πxdxdtdt+(x2−y2)dydtdt=∫02π(xdxdt+(x2−y2)dydt)dt=∫02πsin⁡(2t)⋅2cos⁡(2t)+(sin2⁡(2t)−12)⋅0dt=∫02π2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)dt=∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y
last_observation.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=sin⁡(2t)i+j for t∈[0,2π]?

a
∫02π2sin⁡(4t)dt
b
∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
c
∫02πsin2⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)−1dt
d
∫02πsin⁡(4t)−cos2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫02πsin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=sin⁡(2t),y(t)=1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(sin⁡(2t))i+ddt(1)j=2cos⁡(2t)i.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy=∫02πxdxdtdt+(x2−y2)dydtdt=∫02π(xdxdt+(x2−y2)dydt)dt=∫02πsin⁡(2t)⋅2cos⁡(2t)+(sin2⁡(2t)−12)⋅0dt=∫02π2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)dt=∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
question.knowledge_point: Constructing a Sum of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

solution.reasoning: Here x=\sin(2t), y=1, dx=2\cos(2t)dt, and dy=0. The integrand becomes 2\sin(2t)\cos(2t)=\sin(4t), giving option b directly. Options a and e also integrate to zero over these bounds, so they have the same numerical value. No Math Academy key for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is parametrized by $r(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,i+j$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Along the curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,y(t)=1.
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)\,j \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,dt+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+({sin}^{2}⁡(2t)-{1}^{2})\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy, where C is parametrized by r(t)=sin⁡(2t)i+j for t∈[0,2π]?

a
∫02π2sin⁡(4t)dt
b
∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
c
∫02πsin2⁡(2t)+sin⁡(2t)−1dt
d
∫02πsin⁡(4t)−cos2⁡(2t)dt
e
∫02πsin⁡(2t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Along the curve, we have x(t)=sin⁡(2t),y(t)=1.

The derivative of r(t) is given by

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(sin⁡(2t))i+ddt(1)j=2cos⁡(2t)i.

Therefore, we can write our line integral as follows:

∫Cxdx+(x2−y2)dy=∫02πxdxdtdt+(x2−y2)dydtdt=∫02π(xdxdt+(x2−y2)dydt)dt=∫02πsin⁡(2t)⋅2cos⁡(2t)+(sin2⁡(2t)−12)⋅0dt=∫02π2sin⁡(2t)cos⁡(2t)dt=∫02πsin⁡(4t)dt
