question.html:
Question 12
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=11−x, the vertical line x=2, and the horizontal line y=−2 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−2−1(1−1y)dy
b
π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy
c
π∫−2−1(1+4y+4y2)dy
d
π∫−2−1(1−2y+1y2)dy
e
π∫−2−1(1+1y)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=11−x⟹x=1−1y

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=−2 to y=−1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=1−1y, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫−2−1[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫−2−1[(2)−(1−1y)]2dy=π∫−2−1(1+1y)2dy=π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: Solving for x gives x=1-1/y. For -2≤y≤-1, the disk radius is 2-(1-1/y)=1+1/y. Squaring yields 1+2/y+1/y^2, so option b gives the volume. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/5d154a914d58f5b695adec9dd873ac067ba8280a4fefffd4f2f5559ff5ee04da.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{1}{1-x},$ the vertical line $x=2,$ and the horizontal line $y=-2$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=2,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=\frac{1}{1-x}\,⟹\,x=1-\frac{1}{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=-2$ to $y=-1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/239113c4d2bbca26c694796f6f17bd26bebf47697dad53f7af832088213fd4c9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=1-\frac{1}{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}{[\,(2)-(1-\frac{1}{y})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}{(1+\frac{1}{y})}^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-2}^{-1}(1+\frac{2}{y}+\frac{1}{{y}^{2}})\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 12
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=11−x, the vertical line x=2, and the horizontal line y=−2 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−2−1(1−1y)dy
b
π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy
c
π∫−2−1(1+4y+4y2)dy
d
π∫−2−1(1−2y+1y2)dy
e
π∫−2−1(1+1y)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=11−x⟹x=1−1y

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=−2 to y=−1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=1−1y, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫−2−1[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫−2−1[(2)−(1−1y)]2dy=π∫−2−1(1+1y)2dy=π∫−2−1(1+2y+1y2)dy.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/293593a043a7713d87a2f8ad8a2eaecee26b34288e4662bb4b2fce834e703e56.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ the vertical line $x=-1$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/600ef6d7265add5c669a29394e45facae040292ce19caad9dcae390979b604b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=\sqrt[3]{y}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt[3]{y})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}+2{y}^{1/3}+1)\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3, the vertical line x=−1 and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−10(2y1/3+1)dy
b
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy
c
π∫−11(−y2/3+2y1/3)dy
d
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3)dy
e
π∫−10(y2/3+1)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=x3⟹x=y3

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=y3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(y3)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(y3+1)2dy=π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/600ef6d7265add5c669a29394e45facae040292ce19caad9dcae390979b604b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=\sqrt[3]{y}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt[3]{y})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}+2{y}^{1/3}+1)\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:

question.html:
Question 13
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3, the vertical line x=−1 and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−10(2y1/3+1)dy
b
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy
c
π∫−11(−y2/3+2y1/3)dy
d
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3)dy
e
π∫−10(y2/3+1)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=x3⟹x=y3

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=y3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(y3)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(y3+1)2dy=π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: Writing the curve as x=y^{1/3}, the disk radius is y^{1/3}-(-1)=y^{1/3}+1 for 0≤y≤1. Its square is y^{2/3}+2y^{1/3}+1, giving option b. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/293593a043a7713d87a2f8ad8a2eaecee26b34288e4662bb4b2fce834e703e56.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y={x}^{3},$ the vertical line $x=-1$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1,$ as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y={x}^{3}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt[3]{y}
$$

 

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/600ef6d7265add5c669a29394e45facae040292ce19caad9dcae390979b604b9.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=\sqrt[3]{y}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\sqrt[3]{y})-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(\sqrt[3]{y}+1)^{2}\,\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}+2{y}^{1/3}+1)\,\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=x3, the vertical line x=−1 and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Which of the following integrals gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫−10(2y1/3+1)dy
b
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy
c
π∫−11(−y2/3+2y1/3)dy
d
π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3)dy
e
π∫−10(y2/3+1)dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=x3⟹x=y3

Also, notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=y3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(y3)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(y3+1)2dy=π∫01(y2/3+2y1/3+1)dy.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/68359143b50b4d6187f2d50793b1d3cb4b48656f1996cd222cb5d07f666b535e.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=-1-x,$ the vertical line $x=-3,$ and the horizontal line $y=0$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-3,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=-1-x\,⟹\,x=-1-y
$$

 

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=-3$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1-y & =-3 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/73d5da7e1bd4b409574f6e9ab034dde51012eb956b3ea72a3529f7d432fe781d.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-3,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=-1-y.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-1-y)-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2-y)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4y+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=−1−x, the vertical line x=−3, and the horizontal line y=0 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−3, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
∫02(y2+2y+2)dy
b
π∫01(2−y)dy
c
∫03(y2−y+2)dy
d
π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy
e
π∫03/2(y2+4y+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=−1−x⟹x=−1−y

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=−3 by solving the following equation:

−1−y=−3y=2

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=2 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=−1−y.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫02[(−1−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫02(2−y)2dy=π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy.

last_observation.name: Question 14
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=-1-x\,⟹\,x=-1-y
$$

 

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=-3$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1-y & =-3 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/73d5da7e1bd4b409574f6e9ab034dde51012eb956b3ea72a3529f7d432fe781d.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-3,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=-1-y.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-1-y)-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2-y)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4y+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 14
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=−1−x, the vertical line x=−3, and the horizontal line y=0 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−3, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
∫02(y2+2y+2)dy
b
π∫01(2−y)dy
c
∫03(y2−y+2)dy
d
π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy
e
π∫03/2(y2+4y+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=−1−x⟹x=−1−y

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=−3 by solving the following equation:

−1−y=−3y=2

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=2 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=−1−y.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫02[(−1−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫02(2−y)2dy=π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: Writing the curve as x=-1-y, the disk radius is (-1-y)-(-3)=2-y. The region spans 0≤y≤2, so V=\pi\int_0^2(2-y)^2\,dy=\pi\int_0^2(y^2-4y+4)\,dy, giving option d. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/68359143b50b4d6187f2d50793b1d3cb4b48656f1996cd222cb5d07f666b535e.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=-1-x,$ the vertical line $x=-3,$ and the horizontal line $y=0$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-3,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=-1-x\,⟹\,x=-1-y
$$

 

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=-3$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1-y & =-3 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/73d5da7e1bd4b409574f6e9ab034dde51012eb956b3ea72a3529f7d432fe781d.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-3,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=-1-y.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{[\,(-1-y)-(-3)\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{(2-y)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}-4y+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=−1−x, the vertical line x=−3, and the horizontal line y=0 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−3, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
∫02(y2+2y+2)dy
b
π∫01(2−y)dy
c
∫03(y2−y+2)dy
d
π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy
e
π∫03/2(y2+4y+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=−1−x⟹x=−1−y

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=−3 by solving the following equation:

−1−y=−3y=2

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=2 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=−1−y.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫02[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫02[(−1−y)−(−3)]2dy=π∫02(2−y)2dy=π∫02(y2−4y+4)dy.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/421d588cd290294cf6471704f2459c22b00c8b47756b808e9da267a8007792b2.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ and the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=2,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
question.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

 

We take the positive sign since $x\ge 0.$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=2$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}} & =2 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=8$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/c762c0e41cf8862535e5241a00149fdc6e409c3f79630a411cff73fcd11759b0.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{[\,(2)-(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}-2)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}(\frac{y}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2 and the vertical lines x=0 and x=2 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01(y4−2y2+4)dy
b
π∫02(y2−2)dy
c
π∫08(y2+2)dy
d
π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy
e
π∫08(4y2+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=2x2⟹x=y2

We take the positive sign since x≥0.

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=2 by solving the following equation:

y2=2y=8

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=8 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y2, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫08[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫08[(2)−(y2)]2dy=π∫08(y2−2)2dy=π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy.

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line
last_observation.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

 

We take the positive sign since $x\ge 0.$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=2$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}} & =2 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=8$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/c762c0e41cf8862535e5241a00149fdc6e409c3f79630a411cff73fcd11759b0.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{[\,(2)-(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}-2)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}(\frac{y}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 15
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2 and the vertical lines x=0 and x=2 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01(y4−2y2+4)dy
b
π∫02(y2−2)dy
c
π∫08(y2+2)dy
d
π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy
e
π∫08(4y2+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=2x2⟹x=y2

We take the positive sign since x≥0.

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=2 by solving the following equation:

y2=2y=8

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=8 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y2, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫08[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫08[(2)−(y2)]2dy=π∫08(y2−2)2dy=π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy.
question.knowledge_point: Identifying an Integral Representing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: For the shaded region, horizontal slices span x=\sqrt{y/2} to x=2, with 0≤y≤8. The disk radius is 2-\sqrt{y/2}, whose square is y/2-4\sqrt{y/2}+4, giving option d. The diagram supplies the lower boundary y=0, omitted from the wording. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/421d588cd290294cf6471704f2459c22b00c8b47756b808e9da267a8007792b2.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ and the vertical lines $x=0$ and $x=2$ is rotated ${360}^{∘}$ about the line $x=2,$ as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of $y:$ 

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

 

We take the positive sign since $x\ge 0.$

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=2$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}} & =2 \\ y & =8\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=8$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/c762c0e41cf8862535e5241a00149fdc6e409c3f79630a411cff73fcd11759b0.png)

 

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=2.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{[\,(2)-(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}})\,]}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}{(\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}-2)}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{8}(\frac{y}{2}-4\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}+4)\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

The region enclosed by the curve y=2x2 and the vertical lines x=0 and x=2 is rotated 360∘ about the line x=2, as shown in the picture. Which of the following gives the volume of the resulting solid?

a
π∫01(y4−2y2+4)dy
b
π∫02(y2−2)dy
c
π∫08(y2+2)dy
d
π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy
e
π∫08(4y2+4)dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since our region rotates about a vertical line, we need to write the equation of the given curve in terms of y:

y=2x2⟹x=y2

We take the positive sign since x≥0.

Now, we want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=2 by solving the following equation:

y2=2y=8

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=8 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y2, and

  • leaves through the right function x=2.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫08[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫08[(2)−(y2)]2dy=π∫08(y2−2)2dy=π∫08(y2−4y2+4)dy.

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=\sqrt[3]{y},$ the vertical line $x=3,$ and the horizontal lines $y=0$ and $y=1.$ Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=3.$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/47b612a3e08ff24055cbffa7d53fb337f1905ec861abd3a8e535088d383162cb.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/1927874f5eca0c18b7b61b37d0e6fac5198ec9dcf89205763e88570287330292.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt[3]{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=3.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(3)-(\sqrt[3]{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[3-\sqrt[3]{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}-6{y}^{1/3}+9)\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2/3}\,\text{d}y-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{1/3}\,\text{d}y+9{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi (\frac{3{y}^{5/3}}{5}{|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{9{y}^{4/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}+9y{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi [(\frac{3}{5}-0)-(\frac{9}{2}-0)+(9-0)] \\  & =\frac{51\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?

Consider the region bounded by the curve x=y3, the vertical line x=3, and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3.

a
51π20
b
15π11
c
π10
d
5π11
e
51π10
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

Notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(3)−(y3)]2dy=π∫01[3−y3]2dy=π∫01(y2/3−6y1/3+9)dy=π(∫01y2/3dy−6∫01y1/3dy+9∫01dy)=π(3y5/35|01−9y4/32|01+9y|01)=π[(35−0)−(92−0)+(9−0)]=51π10.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/47b612a3e08ff24055cbffa7d53fb337f1905ec861abd3a8e535088d383162cb.png)

Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/1927874f5eca0c18b7b61b37d0e6fac5198ec9dcf89205763e88570287330292.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=\sqrt[3]{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=3.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(3)-(\sqrt[3]{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[3-\sqrt[3]{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2/3}-6{y}^{1/3}+9)\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2/3}\,\text{d}y-6{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{1/3}\,\text{d}y+9{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi (\frac{3{y}^{5/3}}{5}{|}_{0}^{1}-{\frac{9{y}^{4/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{1}+9y{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi [(\frac{3}{5}-0)-(\frac{9}{2}-0)+(9-0)] \\  & =\frac{51\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 16
?

Consider the region bounded by the curve x=y3, the vertical line x=3, and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3.

a
51π20
b
15π11
c
π10
d
5π11
e
51π10
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

Notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(3)−(y3)]2dy=π∫01[3−y3]2dy=π∫01(y2/3−6y1/3+9)dy=π(∫01y2/3dy−6∫01y1/3dy+9∫01dy)=π(3y5/35|01−9y4/32|01+9y|01)=π[(35−0)−(92−0)+(9−0)]=51π10.
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: The disk radius is 3-y^{1/3} for 0≤y≤1. Thus V=\pi\int_0^1(9-6y^{1/3}+y^{2/3})\,dy=\pi(9-9/2+3/5)=51\pi/10, giving option e. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

Question 16

Consider the region bounded by the curve x=y3, the vertical line x=3, and the horizontal lines y=0 and y=1. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 2π radians about the line x=3.

a
51π20
b
15π11
c
π10
d
5π11
e
51π10
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

Notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=y3, and

  • leaves through the right function x=3.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(3)−(y3)]2dy=π∫01[3−y3]2dy=π∫01(y2/3−6y1/3+9)dy=π(∫01y2/3dy−6∫01y1/3dy+9∫01dy)=π(3y5/35|01−9y4/32|01+9y|01)=π[(35−0)−(92−0)+(9−0)]=51π10.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/5453dfc44e11cad377c1e8e2c30fc23d537d4423d38fab4428395362f51d9412.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={y}^{2}+1,$ the vertical line $x=5,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=5.$

$V=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersection of the curve and the line $x=5$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}+1 & =5 \\ {y}^{2} & =4 \\ y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Since $y\ge 0,$ the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=2$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/e83c5729ef5db920a0b451a8571ad84f45d2b4e950ab831ced0da2c0a12cea50.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={y}^{2}+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=5.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}[\,5-({y}^{2}+1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(16-8{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(16y-\frac{8}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5})|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\pi (32-\frac{64}{3}+\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =\frac{256\pi }{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 256π15​

question.name: Question 18
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/144259aa150936de0e3425c13f953da0833d87c2aba1304aa39b3c47fda03550.png)

The region enclosed by the curve $x=6\sqrt{y}+1,$ the horizontal line $y=1,$  the horizontal line $y=0,$ and the vertical line $x=-1$ is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=-1$, as shown above. Find the volume of the resulting solid.
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left function and which is the right, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/8a17502c300fae56e9f2e1706d23a3e5a7d3233eebff9a77958d117a0135adb0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=6\sqrt{y}+1.$

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(6\sqrt{y}+1)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{y}+2)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24\sqrt{y}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24{y}^{1/2}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(36\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+24\cdot \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}+4y)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(18(1)^{2}+16(1)^{3/2}+4(1))-0] \\  & =38\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

The region enclosed by the curve x=6y+1, the horizontal line y=1, the horizontal line y=0, and the vertical line x=−1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
24π
b
25π4
c
13π2
d
38π
e
36π
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left function and which is the right, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=6y+1.

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(6y+1)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(6y+2)2dy=π∫01(36y+24y+4)dy=π∫01(36y+24y1/2+4)dy=π(36⋅12y2+24⋅23y3/2+4y)|01=π[(18(1)2+16(1)3/2+4(1))−0]=38π.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Notice that the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left function and which is the right, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/8a17502c300fae56e9f2e1706d23a3e5a7d3233eebff9a77958d117a0135adb0.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=-1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=6\sqrt{y}+1.$

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(6\sqrt{y}+1)-(-1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(6\sqrt{y}+2)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24\sqrt{y}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(36y+24{y}^{1/2}+4)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {(36\cdot \frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+24\cdot \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}+4y)|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(18(1)^{2}+16(1)^{3/2}+4(1))-0] \\  & =38\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

The region enclosed by the curve x=6y+1, the horizontal line y=1, the horizontal line y=0, and the vertical line x=−1 is rotated 2π radians about the line x=−1, as shown above. Find the volume of the resulting solid.

a
24π
b
25π4
c
13π2
d
38π
e
36π
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Notice that the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left function and which is the right, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=−1, and

  • leaves through the right function x=6y+1.

Therefore, the volume of the resulting solid is given by

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(6y+1)−(−1)]2dy=π∫01(6y+2)2dy=π∫01(36y+24y+4)dy=π∫01(36y+24y1/2+4)dy=π(36⋅12y2+24⋅23y3/2+4y)|01=π[(18(1)2+16(1)3/2+4(1))−0]=38π.

question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/4643824b623d5325f53407147f086a95073db91be0148381780668c420ec7c45.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x={e}^{y},$ the vertical line $x=e,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=e.$
question.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=e$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y} & =e \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/93fd0875ea2ba1d1d92bb781a61cfb114ac88b7d240cd825b4842f686f7c760f.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={e}^{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=e.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(e)-({e}^{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[e-{e}^{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2}-2{e}^{y+1}+{e}^{2y})\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y+1}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}y\,{|}_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{y+1}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{{e}^{2y}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi (({e}^{2}-0)-2({e}^{2}-e)+(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\pi (-{e}^{2}+2e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{(4e-{e}^{2}-1)\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(-1+4e-{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Consider the region bounded by the curve x=ey, the vertical line x=e, and the horizontal line y=0, as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 2π radians about the line x=e.

a
πe1+4e2
b
π2(4−e)
c
π2(16−e2)
d
πe2
e
π2(−1+4e−e2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=e by solving the following equation:

ey=ey=1

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=ey, and

  • leaves through the right function x=e.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(e)−(ey)]2dy=π∫01[e−ey]2dy=π∫01(e2−2ey+1+e2y)dy=π(e2∫01dy−2∫01ey+1dy+∫01e2ydy)=π(e2y|01−2ey+1|01+e2y2|01)=π((e2−0)−2(e2−e)+(e22−12))=π(−e2+2e+e22−12)=(4e−e2−1)π2=π2(−1+4e−e2).

last_observation.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line $x=e$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{y} & =e \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=1$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/93fd0875ea2ba1d1d92bb781a61cfb114ac88b7d240cd825b4842f686f7c760f.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={e}^{y},$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=e.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}[\,(e)-({e}^{y})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}{[e-{e}^{y}]}^{2}\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{2}-2{e}^{y+1}+{e}^{2y})\text{d}y \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{y+1}\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\pi ({e}^{2}y\,{|}_{0}^{1}-2{e}^{y+1}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{{e}^{2y}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1}) \\  & =\pi (({e}^{2}-0)-2({e}^{2}-e)+(\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\pi (-{e}^{2}+2e+\frac{{e}^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{(4e-{e}^{2}-1)\pi }{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(-1+4e-{e}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

- *enters* the region through the left function $x={e}^{y},$ and

$$

Question 19
?

Consider the region bounded by the curve x=ey, the vertical line x=e, and the horizontal line y=0, as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated 2π radians about the line x=e.

a
πe1+4e2
b
π2(4−e)
c
π2(16−e2)
d
πe2
e
π2(−1+4e−e2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=e by solving the following equation:

ey=ey=1

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

The horizontal arrow

  • enters the region through the left function x=ey, and

  • leaves through the right function x=e.

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

V=π∫01[(right function)−(left function)]2dy=π∫01[(e)−(ey)]2dy=π∫01[e−ey]2dy=π∫01(e2−2ey+1+e2y)dy=π(e2∫01dy−2∫01ey+1dy+∫01e2ydy)=π(e2y|01−2ey+1|01+e2y2|01)=π((e2−0)−2(e2−e)+(e22−12))=π(−e2+2e+e22−12)=(4e−e2−1)π2=π2(−1+4e−e2).
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Volume of a Solid Generated by Rotation About a Vertical Line

solution.reasoning: The intersection e^y=e gives y=1. The disk radius is e-e^y, so V=\pi\int_0^1(e-e^y)^2\,dy=\pi[e^2y-2e^{y+1}+e^{2y}/2]_0^1=\frac{\pi}{2}(-1+4e-e^2), giving option e. No current Math Academy answer or grade is captured.

EXPLANATION

We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersections of the curve and the line x=e by solving the following equation:

ey=ey=1

So, the limits of integration are from y=0 to y=1 along the y-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.

  • leaves through the right function x=e.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/9d8f2d52a0d943a4eeb1d323cc90db145c9b87b57e87d595a7ca5809498e7a6a.png)

Consider the region bounded by the curve $x=y+1,$ the vertical line $x=4,$ and the horizontal line $y=0,$ as shown in the picture. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when that region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the line $x=4.$

$V=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
We want to determine the limits of integration. We find the intersection of the curve and the line $x=4$ by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+1 & =4 \\ y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the limits of integration are from $y=0$ to $y=3$ along the $y$-axis.

To determine which is the left and which is the right function, let's draw our horizontal arrow.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14222139/assets/f9fd1773b9599b1a4b61fc58c854bf998ed147a9707f719a80a3588874c0eb4f.png)

The horizontal arrow 

- *enters* the region through the left function $x=y+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the right function $x=4.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}[(\text{right function})-(\text{left function})\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}[4-(y+1)\,]^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(3-y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}(3-y)^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{3}(0-{3}^{3}) \\  & =9\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 9π

Which of the above could be the graph of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall some of the basic properties of $y=\sqrt[3]{x}.$

- The point $(0,0)$ lies on the graph

- Its domain is $x\in (-\infty ,\infty )$

- Its range is $y\in (-\infty ,\infty )$

- The graph lies in the first and third quadrants

- The function is increasing throughout its entire domain

- As $x\to \infty $, we have $y\to \infty ,$ though it does so slowly

- As $x\to -\infty $, we have $y\to -\infty ,$ though it does so slowly

Of the given options, only graph I has all of the above properties. Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14222393/assets/9a2fe4ad55bbc2853ce6f0507780292ae01616df0a2595ff108e674eb91b2557.png)

What is the length of $\overset{―}{AB}?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the figure, we note that the points $A$ and $B$ have coordinates ${{(4,2)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{,}\,{y}_{1})}$ and ${{(8,3)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{,}\,{y}_{2})},$ respectively. 

To find the distance $AB,$ we can use the distance formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(8-4)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+1} \\  & =\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
From the figure, we note that the points $D$ and $E$ have coordinates ${{(-4,0)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{1}\text{,}\,{y}_{1})}$ and ${{(0,3)}_{⏟}}_{\text{(}{x}_{2}\text{,}\,{y}_{2})},$  respectively.

To find the length of $\overset{―}{DE},$ we use the distance formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}DE & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0-(-4))^{2}+(3-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}+(3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we have (−9,2)⏟(x1,y1) and (−12,−4)⏟(x2,y2). So, the distance d can be calculated using the distance formula, as follows:

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$

questions.raw_html:
1.Finding a Position Vector Given an Acceleration Vector?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨2,2⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−10,−8) and has velocity ⟨0,0⟩ when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-4,-8⟩$ when $t=1,$ find the times when the particle is at the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-4,\,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-4,\,-8⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-1,-4)$ and has velocity $⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Do not round the answers.

$r\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨${{field-1}},{{field-2}}$⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,2+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}-2⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t,\,4t⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-12,\,-8⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the particle is at the origin when $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 6t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-12,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-12,-8⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-12$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-12 & =3(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2, \\ 2{t}^{2}-8 & =2(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle is at the origin when $t=-2$ and $t=2.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}

$$

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.

question.html:
Question 1
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨2,2⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−10,−8) and has velocity ⟨0,0⟩ when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2−4t+1,t2−4t+1⟩
b
r=⟨t2−4t−3,t2−4t+3⟩
c
r=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩
d
r=⟨t2−6t−3,t2−6t+3⟩
e
r=⟨t2−4t−1,t2−4t+1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2,2⟩dt=⟨∫2dt,∫2dt⟩=⟨2t+C1,2t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

v(3)=⟨2(3)+C1,2(3)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨6+C1,6+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−6 and C2=−6. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−6)dt,∫(2t−6)dt⟩=⟨t2−6t+C3,t2−6t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨−10,−8⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

r(3)=⟨(3)2−6(3)+C3,(3)2−6(3)+C4⟩⟨−10,−8⟩=⟨−9+C3,−9+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=−1 and C4=1. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-4,\,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-4,\,-8⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-4,-8⟩$ when $t=1,$ find the times when the particle is at the origin.
question.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-4,\,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-4,\,-8⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v(t)=⟨2t−2,2t⟩,t∈(−∞,∞). Given that the particle is at the position r=⟨−4,−8⟩ when t=1, find the times when the particle is at the origin.

a
t=2
b
t=0
c
The particle is never at the origin
d
t=3
e
t=5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The particle is at the origin when its position is r=⟨0,0⟩. So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−2,2t⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−2)dt,∫2tdt⟩=⟨t2−2t+C1,t2+C2⟩.

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨−4,−8⟩. Substituting t=1, we get

r(1)=⟨(1)2−2(1)+C1,(1)2+C2⟩⟨−4,−8⟩=⟨−1+C1,1+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−3 and C2=−9. Therefore, the position of P at time t is given by

r(t)=⟨t2−2t−3,t2−9⟩.

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation r(t)=0.

r(t)=0⟨t2−2t−3,t2−9⟩=⟨0,0⟩.

So we need t2−2t−3=(t−3)(t+1)=0⇒t=−1,3,t2−9=(t+3)(t−3)=0⇒t=±3.

The only solution that satisfies both equations is t=3.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨12t2,−e−t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−1,−4) and has velocity ⟨0,1⟩ when t=0, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
b
r(t)=⟨−4t4−1,e−t−5⟩
c
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,2e−t−6⟩
d
r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
e
r(t)=⟨t4−1,e−t−5⟩

EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨12t2,−e−t⟩dt=⟨∫12t2dt,∫(−e−t)dt⟩=⟨4t3+C1,e−t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(0)=⟨0,1⟩. Substituting t=0, we get v(0)=⟨4(03)+C1,e−0+C2⟩⟨0,1⟩=⟨C1,1+C2⟩, so we must have C1=0 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity vector is v(t)=⟨4t3,e−t⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector. r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨4t3,e−t⟩dt=⟨∫4t3dt,∫e−tdt⟩=⟨t4+C3,−e−t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨−1,−4⟩. Substituting t=0, we get r(0)=⟨04+C3,−e−0+C4⟩⟨−1,−4⟩=⟨C3,−1+C4⟩, so we must have C3=−1 and C4=−3. Therefore, the position of P at time t is r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩.

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 6t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-12,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-12,-8⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-12$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-12 & =3(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2, \\ 2{t}^{2}-8 & =2(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle is at the origin when $t=-2$ and $t=2.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$

Question 1
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨2,2⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−10,−8) and has velocity ⟨0,0⟩ when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2−4t+1,t2−4t+1⟩
b
r=⟨t2−4t−3,t2−4t+3⟩
c
r=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩
d
r=⟨t2−6t−3,t2−6t+3⟩
e
r=⟨t2−4t−1,t2−4t+1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2,2⟩dt=⟨∫2dt,∫2dt⟩=⟨2t+C1,2t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

v(3)=⟨2(3)+C1,2(3)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨6+C1,6+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−6 and C2=−6. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−6)dt,∫(2t−6)dt⟩=⟨t2−6t+C3,t2−6t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨−10,−8⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

r(3)=⟨(3)2−6(3)+C3,(3)2−6(3)+C4⟩⟨−10,−8⟩=⟨−9+C3,−9+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=−1 and C4=1. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨2,2⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−10,−8) and has velocity ⟨0,0⟩ when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2−4t+1,t2−4t+1⟩
b
r=⟨t2−4t−3,t2−4t+3⟩
c
r=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩
d
r=⟨t2−6t−3,t2−6t+3⟩
e
r=⟨t2−4t−1,t2−4t+1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2,2⟩dt=⟨∫2dt,∫2dt⟩=⟨2t+C1,2t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

v(3)=⟨2(3)+C1,2(3)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨6+C1,6+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−6 and C2=−6. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−6)dt,∫(2t−6)dt⟩=⟨t2−6t+C3,t2−6t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨−10,−8⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

r(3)=⟨(3)2−6(3)+C3,(3)2−6(3)+C4⟩⟨−10,−8⟩=⟨−9+C3,−9+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=−1 and C4=1. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩.

solution.reasoning: Integrating acceleration gives v(t)=⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩ because v(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Thus r(t)=⟨t²−6t+C₁,t²−6t+C₂⟩. Applying r(3)=⟨−10,−8⟩ gives C₁=−1 and C₂=1, so option c is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨2,2⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-10,-8)$ and has velocity $⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=3,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2,2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 2\,\text{d}t,\int 2\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+{C}_{1},\,2t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(3)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(3) & =⟨2(3)+{C}_{1},\,2(3)+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-6$ and ${C}_{2}=-6.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩.
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-6,\,2t-6⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t,\int (2t-6)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{3},\,{t}^{2}-6t+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(3)=⟨-10,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(3) & =⟨(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{3},\,(3)^{2}-6(3)+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-10,-8⟩ & =⟨-9+{C}_{3},\,-9+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=1.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-6t-1,\,{t}^{2}-6t+1⟩.
$$

Question 1
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨2,2⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−10,−8) and has velocity ⟨0,0⟩ when t=3, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r=⟨t2−4t+1,t2−4t+1⟩
b
r=⟨t2−4t−3,t2−4t+3⟩
c
r=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩
d
r=⟨t2−6t−3,t2−6t+3⟩
e
r=⟨t2−4t−1,t2−4t+1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector.

v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨2,2⟩dt=⟨∫2dt,∫2dt⟩=⟨2t+C1,2t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(3)=⟨0,0⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

v(3)=⟨2(3)+C1,2(3)+C2⟩⟨0,0⟩=⟨6+C1,6+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−6 and C2=−6. Therefore, the velocity vector is

v(t)=⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−6,2t−6⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−6)dt,∫(2t−6)dt⟩=⟨t2−6t+C3,t2−6t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(3)=⟨−10,−8⟩. Substituting t=3, we get

r(3)=⟨(3)2−6(3)+C3,(3)2−6(3)+C4⟩⟨−10,−8⟩=⟨−9+C3,−9+C4⟩,

so we must have C3=−1 and C4=1. Therefore, the position of P at time t is

r(t)=⟨t2−6t−1,t2−6t+1⟩.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-4,-8⟩$ when $t=1,$ find the times when the particle is at the origin.
question.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨2t-2,2t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (2t-2)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t+{C}_{1},\,{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-4,\,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨(1)^{2}-2(1)+{C}_{1},\,(1)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-4,\,-8⟩ & =⟨-1+{C}_{1},\,1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=-3$ and ${C}_{2}=-9.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3.$

\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =0 \\ ⟨{t}^{2}-2t-3,\,{t}^{2}-9⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}-2t-3=(t-3)(t+1) & =0\,⇒\,t=-1,3, \\ {t}^{2}-9=(t+3)(t-3) & =0\,⇒\,t=\pm 3.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution that satisfies both equations is $t=3.$
