question.html:
Question 2
?

The velocity v at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by v(t)=⟨2t−2,2t⟩,t∈(−∞,∞). Given that the particle is at the position r=⟨−4,−8⟩ when t=1, find the times when the particle is at the origin.

a
t=2
b
t=0
c
The particle is never at the origin
d
t=3
e
t=5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The particle is at the origin when its position is r=⟨0,0⟩. So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨2t−2,2t⟩dt=⟨∫(2t−2)dt,∫2tdt⟩=⟨t2−2t+C1,t2+C2⟩.

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨−4,−8⟩. Substituting t=1, we get

r(1)=⟨(1)2−2(1)+C1,(1)2+C2⟩⟨−4,−8⟩=⟨−1+C1,1+C2⟩,

so we must have C1=−3 and C2=−9. Therefore, the position of P at time t is given by

r(t)=⟨t2−2t−3,t2−9⟩.

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation r(t)=0.

r(t)=0⟨t2−2t−3,t2−9⟩=⟨0,0⟩.

So we need t2−2t−3=(t−3)(t+1)=0⇒t=−1,3,t2−9=(t+3)(t−3)=0⇒t=±3.

The only solution that satisfies both equations is t=3.

solution.reasoning: Integrating velocity gives r(t)=⟨t²−2t+C₁,t²+C₂⟩. The condition r(1)=⟨−4,−8⟩ yields C₁=−3 and C₂=−9. At the origin, (t−3)(t+1)=0 and (t−3)(t+3)=0 simultaneously, whose only common solution is t=3. Thus option d is mathematically correct; Math Academy's answer key is not captured.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-1,-4)$ and has velocity $⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨12t2,−e−t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−1,−4) and has velocity ⟨0,1⟩ when t=0, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
b
r(t)=⟨−4t4−1,e−t−5⟩
c
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,2e−t−6⟩
d
r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
e
r(t)=⟨t4−1,e−t−5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨12t2,−e−t⟩dt=⟨∫12t2dt,∫(−e−t)dt⟩=⟨4t3+C1,e−t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(0)=⟨0,1⟩. Substituting t=0, we get v(0)=⟨4(03)+C1,e−0+C2⟩⟨0,1⟩=⟨C1,1+C2⟩, so we must have C1=0 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity vector is v(t)=⟨4t3,e−t⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector. r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨4t3,e−t⟩dt=⟨∫4t3dt,∫e−tdt⟩=⟨t4+C3,−e−t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨−1,−4⟩. Substituting t=0, we get r(0)=⟨04+C3,−e−0+C4⟩⟨−1,−4⟩=⟨C3,−1+C4⟩, so we must have C3=−1 and C4=−3. Therefore, the position of P at time t is r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩.

last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

The acceleration a at time t of a particle P moving in the xy-plane is given by a(t)=⟨12t2,−e−t⟩. Given that the particle is at the position (−1,−4) and has velocity ⟨0,1⟩ when t=0, calculate the position vector of P at time t.

a
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
b
r(t)=⟨−4t4−1,e−t−5⟩
c
r(t)=⟨2t4−1,2e−t−6⟩
d
r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩
e
r(t)=⟨t4−1,e−t−5⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. v(t)=∫a(t)dt=∫⟨12t2,−e−t⟩dt=⟨∫12t2dt,∫(−e−t)dt⟩=⟨4t3+C1,e−t+C2⟩

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that v(0)=⟨0,1⟩. Substituting t=0, we get v(0)=⟨4(03)+C1,e−0+C2⟩⟨0,1⟩=⟨C1,1+C2⟩, so we must have C1=0 and C2=0. Therefore, the velocity vector is v(t)=⟨4t3,e−t⟩.

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector. r(t)=∫v(t)dt=∫⟨4t3,e−t⟩dt=⟨∫4t3dt,∫e−tdt⟩=⟨t4+C3,−e−t+C4⟩

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that r(0)=⟨−1,−4⟩. Substituting t=0, we get r(0)=⟨04+C3,−e−0+C4⟩⟨−1,−4⟩=⟨C3,−1+C4⟩, so we must have C3=−1 and C4=−3. Therefore, the position of P at time t is r(t)=⟨t4−1,−e−t−3⟩.

solution.reasoning: Integrating acceleration and applying v(0)=⟨0,1⟩ gives v(t)=⟨4t³,e^(−t)⟩. Integrating again gives r(t)=⟨t⁴+C₁,−e^(−t)+C₂⟩. Since r(0)=⟨−1,−4⟩, C₁=−1 and C₂=−3. Option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $(-1,-4)$ and has velocity $⟨0,1⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position vector of $P$ at time $t.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector. To find the velocity vector, we first need to integrate the acceleration vector. 

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨12{t}^{2},-{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 12{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (-{e}^{-t})\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},{e}^{-t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(0)=⟨0,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(0) & =⟨4({0}^{3})+{C}_{1},{e}^{-0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,1⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},1+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=0.$ Therefore, the velocity vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can compute the position vector by integrating the velocity vector.

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨4{t}^{3},{e}^{-t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-t}+{C}_{4}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-1,-4⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{4}+{C}_{3},-{e}^{-0}+{C}_{4}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,-4⟩ & =⟨{C}_{3},-1+{C}_{4}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{3}=-1$ and ${C}_{4}=-3.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{t}^{4}-1,-{e}^{-t}-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩.
$$

Given that the particle is at the position $r=⟨0,0⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the position of $P$ at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Do not round the answers.

$r\,(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨${{field-1}},{{field-2}}$⟩$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{t}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨0,0⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0+{C}_{1},\,2{e}^{0}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨0,0⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,2+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=0$ and ${C}_{2}=-2.$ Therefore, the position vector at time $t$ is given by

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2{e}^{t}-2⟩.
$$

To find the position vector at time $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we substitute $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ into the above, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨sin\,(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2{e}^{\pi /2}-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t,\,4t⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-12,\,-8⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the particle is at the origin when $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 6t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-12,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-12,-8⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-12$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-12 & =3(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2, \\ 2{t}^{2}-8 & =2(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle is at the origin when $t=-2$ and $t=2.$

feedback.problem:
The velocity $v$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
v(t)=⟨6t,\,4t⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Given that the particle is at the position  $r=⟨-12,\,-8⟩$ when $t=0,$ calculate the times when the particle is at the origin. Do not round the answers.

In **ascending order**, the particle is at the origin when $t=$
{{field-1}}
and $t=$
{{field-2}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
The particle is at the origin when its position is $r=⟨0,0⟩.$ So first, we need to compute the position function of the particle.

To compute the position vector, we need to integrate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\int v(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨6t,\,4t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int 6t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2{t}^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $r(0)=⟨-12,-8⟩.$ Substituting $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨3(0)^{2}+{C}_{1},\,2(0)^{2}+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-12,-8⟩ & =⟨{C}_{1},\,{C}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we must have ${C}_{1}=-12$ and ${C}_{2}=-8.$ Therefore, the position of $P$ at time $t$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the times at which the particle is at the origin, we solve the equation $r(t)=⟨0,0⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3{t}^{2}-12,\,2{t}^{2}-8⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}-12 & =3(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2, \\ 2{t}^{2}-8 & =2(t-2)(t+2)=0\,⇒\,t=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in ascending order, the particle is at the origin when $t=-2$ and $t=2.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$

$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$

questions.raw_html:
2.Proving the First Shifting Theorem?

Consider a function z(t) such that its Laplace transform is L{z(t)}=Z(s) for s>s0. Suppose we wish to find L{e6tz(t)}. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

est⋅e6tz(t)
e−st⋅e6tz(t)
e−st⋅e−6tz(t)
est⋅e6tz(t)
est⋅e−6tz(t)
e−(s−6)t
e−(s−6)t
e−(s+6)t
e(s−6)t
e(s+6)t
Z(s−6)
Z(s−6)
Z(s+6)
Z(s)
s>s0+6
s>s0+6
s>s0
s>s0−6
L{e6tz(t)}=∫0∞{(e−st⋅e6tz(t))(S0)}dt=∫0∞{(e−(s−6)t)(S1)}z(t)dt={(Z(s−6))(S2)}for{(s>s0+6)(S3)}.

questions.problem:
Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $5$ units to the right.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e−2t+2te2t for s>2.

a
1(s+2)2+2s−2
b
2(s+2)2+1s−2
c
2(s+2)2(s−2)
d
1s+2+2(s−2)2
e
2(s+2)(s−2)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t+2te2t}=L{e−2t}+L{2te2t}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te2t}=1(s−2)2.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}=1s+2+2⋅1(s−2)2=1s+2+2(s−2)2.

This transform is valid for s>2.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.
$$

question.problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.

EXPLANATION

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

L{e−5tz(t)}=∫0∞e−st⋅e−5tz(t)dt=∫0∞e−(s+5)tz(t)dt

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $5$ units to the right.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
question.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

Question 4
?

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e5tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the right.
b
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 5 horizontally.
c
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
d
Shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the left.
e
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 5 vertically.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e5tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the right.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}$ for $s>2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

Question 1
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e−2t+2te2t for s>2.

a
1(s+2)2+2s−2
b
2(s+2)2+1s−2
c
2(s+2)2(s−2)
d
1s+2+2(s−2)2
e
2(s+2)(s−2)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t+2te2t}=L{e−2t}+L{2te2t}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te2t}=1(s−2)2.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}=1s+2+2⋅1(s−2)2=1s+2+2(s−2)2.

This transform is valid for s>2.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}+2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+L\{2t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t\} & =\frac{1}{{s}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{t{e}^{2t}\} & =\frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{-2t}\}+2L\{t{e}^{2t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{(s-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+2}+\frac{2}{(s-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>2.$

EXPLANATION

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t+2te2t}=L{e−2t}+L{2te2t}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te2t}=1(s−2)2.

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}=1s+2+2⋅1(s−2)2=1s+2+2(s−2)2.

Question 1
?

Given that L{tn}=n!sn+1,s>0, use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of f(t)=e−2t+2te2t for s>2.

a
1(s+2)2+2s−2
b
2(s+2)2+1s−2
c
2(s+2)2(s−2)
d
1s+2+2(s−2)2
e
2(s+2)(s−2)2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t+2te2t}=L{e−2t}+L{2te2t}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}

We are given that, for s>0, L{tn}=n!sn+1.

Therefore, we have the following: L{t}=1s2

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a). Therefore, L{te2t}=1(s−2)2.

Therefore, the Laplace transform of f(t) is

L{f(t)}=L{e−2t}+2L{te2t}=1s+2+2⋅1(s−2)2=1s+2+2(s−2)2.

This transform is valid for s>2.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$

Consider a function z(t) such that its Laplace transform is L{z(t)}=Z(s) for s>s0. Suppose we wish to find L{e6tz(t)}. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write

est⋅e6tz(t)
est⋅e6tz(t)
e−st⋅e6tz(t)
est⋅e−6tz(t)
e−st⋅e−6tz(t)
e−(s−6)t
e(s+6)t
e(s−6)t
e−(s+6)t
e−(s−6)t
Z(s−6)
Z(s)
Z(s+6)
Z(s−6)
s>s0+6
s>s0−6
s>s0+6
s>s0
L{e6tz(t)}=∫0∞{(est⋅e6tz(t))(S0)}dt=∫0∞{(e(s+6)t)(S1)}z(t)dt={(Z(s))(S2)}for{(s>s0−6)(S3)}.

EXPLANATION

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

L{e6tz(t)}=∫0∞e−st⋅e6tz(t)dt=∫0∞e−(s−6)tz(t)dt

Now, recall that Z(s)=∫0∞e−stz(t)dt, where s>s0. Therefore, ∫0∞e−(s−6)tz(t)dt=Z(s−6), where s−6>s0⇒s>s0+6.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

where 

$$
s-6>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+6.
$$

Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{6t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{6t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-6)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s-6),
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.
$$

e−(s+5)t
Z(s+5)
Z(s+5)
Z(s−5)

L{e−5tz(t)}=∫0∞{(e−st⋅e5tz(t))(S0)}dt=∫0∞{(e(s+5)t)(S1)}z(t)dt={(Z(s+5))(S2)}for{(s>s0)(S3)}.

EXPLANATION

Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

L{e−5tz(t)}=∫0∞e−st⋅e−5tz(t)dt=∫0∞e−(s+5)tz(t)dt

Now, recall that Z(s)=∫0∞e−stz(t)dt, where s>s0. Therefore, ∫0∞e−(s+5)tz(t)dt=Z(s+5), where s+5>s0⇒s>s0−5.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

where 

$$
s+5>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-5.
$$

Consider a function $z(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L\{z(t)\}=Z(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.

By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{e}^{-5t}z(t)\} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-5t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Z(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+5)t}\,z(t)\,\text{d}t=Z(s+5),
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L\{f(t)\}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
question.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$
then
$L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L\{{e}^{5t}f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $5$ units to the right.

Question 4
?

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e5tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the right.
b
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 5 horizontally.
c
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
d
Shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the left.
e
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 5 vertically.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e5tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 5 units to the right.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider a function f(t) for which the Laplace transform is L{f(t)}=F(s). How can we obtain the graph of L{e6tf(t)} from the graph of F(s)?

a
Shift the graph of F(s) by 6 units to the left.
b
The Laplace transform is unchanged.
c
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 6 horizontally.
d
Scale the graph of F(s) by a scale factor of 6 vertically.
e
Shift the graph of F(s) by 6 units to the right.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The first shifting theorem states that if L{f(t)}=F(s), then L{eatf(t)}=F(s−a).

This implies that multiplying a function f(t) by eat shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the s-axis.

  • If a>0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the right.

  • If a<0, the graph of F(s) shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of L{e6tf(t)}, we must shift the graph of F(s) by 6 units to the right.

solution.reasoning: The first shifting theorem gives L{e^{6t}f(t)}=F(s-6), whose graph is F(s) shifted 6 units to the right. Thus option e is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

answers.correct_value: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $6$ units to the right.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.$ Does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[n]{3}\cdot {n}^{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{n-1/2}} \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}=1.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.$ Does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{11}{7\cdot \sqrt[n]{n!}}) \\  & =\frac{11}{7}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}} \\  & =\frac{11}{7}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}}=0.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.
$$

$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[n]{3}\cdot {n}^{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{n-1/2}} \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}=1.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=nn/23nn2. Does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=nn/23nn2.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(nn/23nn2)1/n=limn→∞n3n⋅nn=limn→∞13n⋅1nn−1/2=1⋅0=0 Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞13n=1.

Since L=0<1, the series converges by the root test.

Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{11}{7\cdot \sqrt[n]{n!}}) \\  & =\frac{11}{7}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}} \\  & =\frac{11}{7}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}}=0.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

an=11n7n⋅n!.

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(11n7n⋅n!)1/n=limn→∞(117⋅n!n)=117limn→∞1n!n=117⋅0=0 Note that we used the fact that

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=6n5nn6. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=1. The root test gives no conclusion.
b
L=∞. The series is divergent.
c
L=65. The series is divergent.
d
L=56. The series is convergent.
e
L=6. The series is divergent.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=6n5nn6.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(6n5nn6)1/n=limn→∞(65⋅n6n)=65limn→∞(1nn)6=65⋅16=65

Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

Since L=65>1, the series diverges by the root test.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[n]{3}\cdot {n}^{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{n-1/2}} \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}=1.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

question.html:
Question 1
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=nn/23nn2. Does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=13. The series is convergent.
b
L=19. The series is convergent.
c
L=3. The series is divergent.
d
L=0. The series is convergent.
e
L=∞. The series is divergent.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=nn/23nn2.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(nn/23nn2)1/n=limn→∞n3n⋅nn=limn→∞13n⋅1nn−1/2=1⋅0=0 Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞13n=1.

Since L=0<1, the series converges by the root test.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{n}^{n/2}}{3{n}^{{n}^{2}}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt[n]{3}\cdot {n}^{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{n-1/2}} \\  & =1\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{3}}=1.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.$ Does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{11}{7\cdot \sqrt[n]{n!}}) \\  & =\frac{11}{7}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}} \\  & =\frac{11}{7}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}}=0.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{11}^{n}}{{7}^{n}\cdot n!})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{11}{7\cdot \sqrt[n]{n!}}) \\  & =\frac{11}{7}{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}} \\  & =\frac{11}{7}\cdot 0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{\frac{1}{n!}}=0.
$$

Since $L=0<1,$ the series converges by the root test.

Question 2
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=11n7n⋅n!. Does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=149. The series is convergent.
b
L=0. The series is convergent.
c
L=117. The series is divergent.
d
L=∞. The series is divergent.
e
L=17. The series is convergent.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=11n7n⋅n!.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(11n7n⋅n!)1/n=limn→∞(117⋅n!n)=117limn→∞1n!n=117⋅0=0 Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞1n!n=0.

Since L=0<1, the series converges by the root test.

solution.reasoning: The nth root is 11/(7(n!)^{1/n}). Since (n!)^{1/n} tends to infinity, L=0. The series therefore converges by the root test. Choice b is mathematically correct, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

question.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=5nnn+1(9+5n)n. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=19. The series is convergent.
b
L=∞. The series is divergent.
c
L=1. The root test gives no conclusion.
d
L=5. The series is divergent.
e
L=1. The series is divergent.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=5nnn+1(9+5n)n.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(5nnn+1(9+5n)n)1/n=limn→∞(5nnn⋅n(9+5n)n)1/n=limn→∞5nnn9+5n=limn→∞(nn⋅5nn)(9n+5nn)=limn→∞5nn(9n+5)=5⋅10+5=55=1 Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

Since L=1, the root test gives no conclusion.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n+1}}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{5}^{n}{n}^{n}\cdot n}{(9+5n)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5n\sqrt[n]{n}}{9+5n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\sqrt[n]{n}\cdot \frac{5n}{n})}{(\frac{9}{n}+\frac{5n}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{5\sqrt[n]{n}}{(\frac{9}{n}+5)} \\  & =\frac{5\cdot 1}{0+5} \\  & =\frac{5}{5} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=1,$ the root test gives no conclusion.

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=5nnn+1(9+5n)n. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=19. The series is convergent.
b

c

d
L=5. The series is divergent.
e
L=1. The series is divergent.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=5nnn+1(9+5n)n.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(5nnn+1(9+5n)n)1/n=limn→∞(5nnn⋅n(9+5n)n)1/n=limn→∞5nnn9+5n=limn→∞(nn⋅5nn)(9n+5nn)=limn→∞5nn(9n+5)=5⋅10+5=55=1 Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{6}{5\cdot \sqrt[n]{{n}^{6}}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n}})}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot {1}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{6}{5}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

choices.value: $L=1.$ The root test gives no conclusion.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=6n5nn6. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
L=1. The root test gives no conclusion.
b
L=∞. The series is divergent.
c
L=65. The series is divergent.
d
L=56. The series is convergent.
e
L=6. The series is divergent.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=6n5nn6.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞(6n5nn6)1/n=limn→∞(65⋅n6n)=65limn→∞(1nn)6=65⋅16=65

Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

Since L=65>1, the series diverges by the root test.

solution.reasoning: The nth root is (6/5)n^{-6/n}. Since n^{-6/n}=exp(-6 log(n)/n) tends to 1, L=6/5>1, so the series diverges by the root test. Choice c is mathematically correct; no Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{{6}^{n}}{{5}^{n}{n}^{6}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{6}{5\cdot \sqrt[n]{{n}^{6}}}) \\  & =\frac{6}{5}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n}})}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\cdot {1}^{6} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{6}{5}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

choices.value: $L=1.$ The root test gives no conclusion.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Calculate $L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ for the sequence ${a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.$ According to the root test, does ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ converge or diverge?
question.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

choices.value: $L=1.$ The root test gives no conclusion.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}$ such that ${a}_{n}\ge 0$ for all $n\ge 1,$ and that $L$ is defined as  

$$
L={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n}.
$$

 

Then, the root test states the following:

- If $L<1$, the series converges.

- If $L>1$ or $L=\infty $, the series diverges.

- If $L=1$, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence ${a}_{n},$ defined as

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}}.
$$

To apply the root test, we find the limit of $\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}}$ as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{{a}_{n}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{({a}_{n})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(\frac{(10n)^{n}n}{(8n+1)^{n}})}^{1/n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{8n+1}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10n\sqrt[n]{n}}{n(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{10\sqrt[n]{n}}{(8+\frac{1}{n})} \\  & =\frac{10\cdot 1}{8+0} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we used the fact that

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }\sqrt[n]{n}=1.
$$

Since $L=\frac{5}{4}>1,$ the series diverges by the root test.

question.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=(10n)nn(8n+1)n. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
 L=1. The root test gives no conclusion.
b
 L=10. The series is divergent.
c
 L=18. The series is convergent.
d
 L=54. The series is divergent.
e
 L=∞. The series is divergent.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=(10n)nn(8n+1)n.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞((10n)nn(8n+1)n)1/n=limn→∞(10nnn8n+1)=limn→∞10nnnn(8+1n)=limn→∞10nn(8+1n)=10⋅18+0=54

Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

Since L=54>1, the series diverges by the root test.

solution.reasoning: The nth root is (10n/(8n+1))n^{1/n}. Since n^{1/n} tends to 1, L=10/8=5/4>1, so the series diverges by the root test. Choice d is mathematically correct; no Math Academy answer-key evidence was supplied.

feedback.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate L=limn→∞ann for the sequence an=(10n)nn(8n+1)n. According to the root test, does ∑n=1∞an converge or diverge?

a
 L=1. The root test gives no conclusion.
b
 L=10. The series is divergent.
c
 L=18. The series is convergent.
d
 L=54. The series is divergent.
e
 L=∞. The series is divergent.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the series ∑n=1∞an such that an≥0 for all n≥1, and that L is defined as

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n.

Then, the root test states the following:

  • If L<1, the series converges.

  • If L>1 or L=∞, the series diverges.

  • If L=1, the root test is inconclusive.

We have the sequence an, defined as

an=(10n)nn(8n+1)n.

To apply the root test, we find the limit of ann as n→∞:

L=limn→∞ann=limn→∞(an)1/n=limn→∞((10n)nn(8n+1)n)1/n=limn→∞(10nnn8n+1)=limn→∞10nnnn(8+1n)=limn→∞10nn(8+1n)=10⋅18+0=54

Note that we used the fact that

limn→∞nn=1.

Since L=54>1, the series diverges by the root test.

questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/275b62fbec1c1a550cb23b481ec54c1e12d3d42e70cf95cd917f1b932638add4.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5))\cdot 0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-1$ at each left endpoint:

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $8$ | $15$ | $24$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+8+15+24)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50\cdot 0.5 \\  & =25\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A speedboat travels downstream on a river. The table below gives the speed $v(t)$, in miles per hour, of the boat at certain moments during its journey.

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)\,(\text{mi/hour})$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ | $80$ |

Use a left Riemann sum for $v(t)$ over the interval $[0,2]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total distance traveled by the speedboat.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=2,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{2-0}{4}=0.5.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v({x}_{0})+v({t}_{1})+…+v({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(v(0)+v(0.5)+v(1)+v(1.5))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(10+35+40+65)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =150\cdot 0.5 \\  & =75\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance traveled by the speedboat. So, the distance is $75\,\text{mi}.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[1,10]$ with a regular step size. Estimate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[1,10]$ using a left Riemann sum with $3$ equal subintervals.

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(4)+f(7))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the interval $[1,10]$ is divided into $3$ equal subintervals, the width of each subinterval is

$$
Δx=\frac{10-1}{3}=3.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at the left endpoints:

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+0)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A tank is filling with soda. The table below gives the rate $R(t)$, in liters per minute, at which the tank is filling at certain moments since it started.

| $t\,(\text{minutes})$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ | $12$ |

Given that the tank is empty when $t=0,$ use a left Riemann sum for $R(t)$ over the interval $[0,12]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total volume of soda in the tank after $12$ minutes.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=12,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{12-0}{4}=3.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R({t}_{0})+R({t}_{1})+…+R({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(R(0)+R(3)+R(6)+R(9))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $R(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)$ | $30$ | $40$ | $60$ | $70$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(30+40+60+70)\cdot 3 \\  & =200\cdot 3 \\  & =600\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total volume in the tank. So, the volume is $600$ liters.

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=3x-{x}^{2}$ over the interval $[0.5,2.5]$ using a left Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/0e3f499cbc36c9dca7e759b67a8fd9e94959039f3403832e1d60b9ed598c44dd.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1.25$ | $2$ | $2.25$ | $2$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1.25+2+2.25+2)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =7.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =3.75\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[-3,3]$ with a regular step size. If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $4$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $5$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(-3)+f(-1)+f(1))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =(5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =10+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be $4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}10+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =-6 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
The following table shows the rate of change of a city's temperature over a $10$-hour period, starting at $2\,\text{a.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{h})$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T\,{(}^{∘}\text{C}/\text{h})$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}$ has a value of $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ what is the value of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=T(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{T({t}_{0})+T({t}_{1})+…+T({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(T(2)+T(4)+T(6)+T(8)+T(10))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $T(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+10) \\  & =2k+20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature is $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+20 & =26 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

John is selling juice at a market stall. The table below gives the rate $r(t)$ of juice sold over a period of $6$ hours, from $1\,\text{p.m.}$ to $7\,\text{p.m.}$

questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=r(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{r({t}_{0})+r({t}_{1})+…+r({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(r(1)+r(3)+r(5))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $r(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)$ | $k$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(k+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+5) \\  & =2k+10\end{aligned}
$$

In the given context, the area under the curve represents the total number of liters sold by John. Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total number of liters sold is $16,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+10 & =16 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[2,8]$ with a regular step size.

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ | $1$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $18$, then what must be the value of $k?$ 

$\,\,k=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+f({x}_{2})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(2)+f(4)+f(6))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the points are $2,4,6,8$ with three subintervals, the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{8-2}{3}=2.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each left-endpoint:

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈((-3)+5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(2+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =4+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A=18$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}4+2k & =18 \\ 2k & =14 \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$
