questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Maya runs a lemonade stand. The table below gives the selling rate $r(t)$ (in liters per hour) over a $6$-hour period starting at noon.

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)\,(\text{L/hour})$ | $1$ | $k$ | $5$ | $3$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total number of liters sold over the $6$-hour period (with three subintervals defined by the given points) is $28$ liters, then what is the value of $k?$ 

$\,\,k=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=r(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{r({t}_{0})+r({t}_{1})+…+r({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(r(0)+r(2)+r(4))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $r(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $r(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $5$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+5)\cdot 2 \\  & =(k+6)\cdot 2 \\  & =2k+12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total number of liters sold by Maya. Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total number of liters sold is $28,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+12 & =28 \\ 2k & =16 \\ k & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/671d5efc8abc559cf638bfbfdda76bddb0b8d5c2d9134dffbbf7eab0e2f0b25a.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $7$ | $17$ | $31$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+7+17+31)\cdot 1 \\  & =56\cdot 1 \\  & =56\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is strictly $\text{increasing}$ over the interval $[1,5],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an $\text{underestimate}$ of the actual area.

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=-{x}^{2}+3x+1$ over the interval $[1.5,3.5]$ using a left Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$ Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/ad1e85721eb2142f5cad422530aeed86c0919f34261d19e11e9f056cf355b387.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5)+f(3)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.25$ | $3$ | $2.25$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.25+3+2.25+1)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =9.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.75\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[1.5,3.5],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area.

14.?

Estimate the area under the curve y=x2−2x+2 over the interval [1,3] using a left Riemann sum with step size Δx=0.5. Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?

questions.name: Question 15
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/e8cd8966d69260c77685d349c97eceb1545686d347f6cdb827ad470880797bf5.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0)+f(0.25)+f(0.5)+f(0.75)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.25$ | $0.5$ | $0.75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+3+4)\cdot 0.25 \\  & =10\cdot 0.25 \\  & =2.5\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is strictly $\text{increasing}$ over the interval $[0,1],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an $\text{underestimate}$ of the actual area.

questions.name: Question 16
questions.problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[0,10].$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $15$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[0,10].$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(0)Δ{x}_{1}+f(3)Δ{x}_{2}+f(5)Δ{x}_{3}+f(7)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $3$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $15$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 3+4\cdot 2+5\cdot 2+9\cdot 3 \\  & =3+8+10+27 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 17
questions.problem:
Daniel decides to go on a diet. The table below gives the rate $w(t)$, in pounds per week, at which he loses weight over a period of $7$ weeks.

| $t\,(\text{week})$ | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $w(t)\,(\text{pounds/week})$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Use a left Riemann sum for $w(t)$ over the interval $[0,7]$ with three subintervals to approximate Daniel's total weight loss.
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈w(0)Δ{t}_{1}+w(1)Δ{t}_{2}+w(3)Δ{t}_{3},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i+1}-{t}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $-$ |
| $w(t)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 4 \\  & =1+4+4 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total weight lost by Daniel. He lost approximately $9$ pounds.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v\,(\text{km/min})$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1.5$ |

Assuming that the family traveled $130\,\text{km}$ during the first hour of the trip, use the left Riemann sum to approximate the total distance traveled during the first two hours.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=5$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈v(60)Δ{t}_{1}+v(70)Δ{t}_{2}+v(80)Δ{t}_{3}+v(95)Δ{t}_{4}+v(110)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i+1}-{t}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $60$ | $70$ | $80$ | $95$ | $110$ | $120$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $10$ | $10$ | $15$ | $15$ | $10$ | $-$ |
| $v(t)$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1.5$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈10\cdot 1.5+10\cdot 2+15\cdot 1+15\cdot 1+10\cdot 2 \\  & =15+20+15+15+20 \\  & =85\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the given context, the area under the curve represents the distance covered in $60$ minutes of travel, from $t=60$ minutes to $t=120$ minutes. The distance traveled in the first two hours is 

$$
\begin{aligned}d=130+85=215\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[-3,5].$

In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(-3)Δ{x}_{1}+f(-1)Δ{x}_{2}+f(0)Δ{x}_{3}+f(3)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $3$ |

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈-1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 3+4\cdot 2 \\  & =-2+1+6+8 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Left Riemann Sum With Regular Step Size
canonical_examples.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=f(x)=(2x-4)^2$ over the interval $[0,2]$ using a left Riemann sum with $4$ rectangles of equal width.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $\Delta x,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=2,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
\Delta x=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{2-0}{4}=0.5.
$$

Now, let's sketch our situation. We are using a left Riemann sum, which means we draw the rectangles so that the left corner of each rectangle coincides with the curve.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/56427bec8108b822c4e1980725073cedc9fc79575d606014f72ea6ca9f8959c2.png)

The area $\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(0)}}+{\color{red}{f(0.5)}}+{\color{red}{f(1)}}+{\color{red}{f(1.5)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $16$ | $9$ | $4$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A≈(16+9+4+1)\cdot 0.5=15\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Solving for an Unknown Given the Value of a Left Riemann Sum With Regular Step Size
canonical_examples.problem:
The table below gives some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[-4,2].$ If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ equal subintervals has a value of $28,$ then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $k$ | $2$ |
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area $\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated using the formula for the left Riemann sum:

$$
\mathcal A\approx(\overbrace{{\color{red}{f(-4)}}+{\color{red}{f(-2)}}+{\color{red}{f(0)}}}^{\color{red}{\large\text{heights}}})\cdot \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}{\large\text{width}}}
$$

So, we set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $5$ | $3$ | $k$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(5+3+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(8+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =16+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are given that $\mathcal A$ must be $28,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}16+2k & =28 \\ 2k & =12 \\ k & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose that we wish to find the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the graph of $y=x^2$ between the $x$-values $x=1$ and $x=4,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/99cee7824a157e5a08292ebba9e60a5633c7a2f8a5ebb496fc1d5dbe14f858e3.png)

We can *approximate* the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/8aa7a3f9be8371b1459874cd2cb8c0c4caf1000d76b99d134fb6e806e638c548.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =1+4+9 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we approximated the area using a **left Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*left* corner of each rectangle touches the curve. 

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles are entirely *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the actual area.

tutorials.name: Overestimates and Underestimates
tutorials.problem:
Whether the left Riemann sum underestimates or overestimates the actual area under a function depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

- If the function $f(x)$ is increasing, then the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/883b1d5faacf246557319e1f2b4fa253a06f657c589b24e5ec27eb35c00528c5.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/ab23c5b0d95a6bd78ac337266bb504c63b528d756548cbcd38e8b236ef140bc3.png)

tutorials.name: Left Riemann Sums with Irregular Step Size
tutorials.problem:
In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta x$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $12$ |

First, note that the domain of $f(x)$ has been *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{
 [1,4] &= [1, 2] \cup [2, 3.5] \cup [3.5, 4] .
}
$$

 

Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/2e8563480f46ff335042c3c52a6f60983f871dccb886c8cf3ca0844504a73db6.png)

  

We've drawn some rectangles to help us calculate our left Riemann sum, and we have chosen the heights of each rectangle to be calculated using the left endpoint of each interval. 

By calculating the area of each rectangle, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/8f62020b1888f7479665b04028acb822fdccfa9049a37e306ea30ce0aa703ac7.svg)

Plugging our numbers into the above, we find

$$
\eqalign{
\mathcal{A}	&\approx	{\color{red}1} \cdot ({\color{blue}2-1})
						+ {\color{red}4} \cdot ({\color{blue}3.5-2})
						+ {\color{red}6} \cdot ({\color{blue}4-3.5}) \[5pt]
			&= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}1} +{\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}1.5}+ {\color{red}6} \cdot {\color{blue}0.5}  \[5pt]
			&=1+6+3\[5pt]
			&= 10.
}
$$

tutorial.name: Introduction
tutorial.problem:
Suppose that we wish to find the area $\mathcal{A}$ under the graph of $y=x^2$ between the $x$-values $x=1$ and $x=4,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/99cee7824a157e5a08292ebba9e60a5633c7a2f8a5ebb496fc1d5dbe14f858e3.png)

We can *approximate* the area using, for instance, the area of three rectangles, each with a width equal to $1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/8aa7a3f9be8371b1459874cd2cb8c0c4caf1000d76b99d134fb6e806e638c548.png)

So, we find the area of each rectangle and then add them all together.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\overset{\text{[math]1[/math]st rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]2[/math]nd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(2)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}}+\overset{\text{[math]3[/math]rd rectangle}}{\overset{⏞}{[\,\overset{\text{height}}{\overset{⏞}{f(3)}}\,\cdot \,{{1}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}\,]}} \\  & =[{1}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{2}^{2}\cdot 1]+[{3}^{2}\cdot 1] \\  & =1+4+9 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we approximated the area using a **left Riemann sum**, which means that the top-*left* corner of each rectangle touches the curve. 

Because the function is *strictly increasing* over the interval $[1,4],$ the rectangles are entirely *below* the function, which means our approximation is an *underestimate* of the actual area.

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$

Question 4
?

A tank is filling with soda. The table below gives the rate R(t), in liters per minute, at which the tank is filling at certain moments since it started.

t(minutes) 0 3 6 9 12
R(t)(liters/minute) 30 40 60 70 90

Given that the tank is empty when t=0, use a left Riemann sum for R(t) over the interval [0,12] with four subintervals to approximate the total volume of soda in the tank after 12 minutes.

a
10000 liters
b
800 liters
c
600 liters
d
2000 liters
e
400 liters
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's compute the step size Δt, which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are a=0 and b=12, and there are n=4 rectangles, so the step size is

Δt=b−an=12−04=3.

The area A can be approximated using the formula

A≈(R(t0)+R(t1)+…+R(tn−1)⏞heights)⋅Δt⏟ width=(R(0)+R(3)+R(6)+R(9))⋅Δt.

So, we now set up a table with the values of R(t) at each point:

t 0 3 6 9
R(t) 30 40 60 70

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area: A≈(30+40+60+70)⋅3=200⋅3=600

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total volume in the tank. So, the volume is 600 liters.

tutorial.name: Overestimates and Underestimates
tutorial.problem:
Whether the left Riemann sum underestimates or overestimates the actual area under a function depends on whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

- If the function $f(x)$ is increasing, then the rectangles fall *below* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *underestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/883b1d5faacf246557319e1f2b4fa253a06f657c589b24e5ec27eb35c00528c5.png)

- If the function $f(x)$ is decreasing, then  the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means the left Riemann sum gives an *overestimate* of the actual area under the curve $y=f(x).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/ab23c5b0d95a6bd78ac337266bb504c63b528d756548cbcd38e8b236ef140bc3.png)

tutorial.name: Left Riemann Sums with Irregular Step Size
tutorial.problem:
In the last few examples, the step size $\Delta x$ was the same for each of the rectangles. In these cases, we say that the step size is **regular**.

There are situations where the step size can vary, which we call an **irregular step size**. But we can still use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area.

For example, let's use a left Riemann sum to approximate the area under the curve of the continuous function $y=f(x)$ whose data is given in the table below.

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3.5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $6$ | $12$ |

First, note that the domain of $f(x)$ has been *partitioned* as 

$$
\eqalign{
 [1,4] &= [1, 2] \cup [2, 3.5] \cup [3.5, 4] .
}
$$

 

Let's plot what this function might look like, using the values given in the table. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/2e8563480f46ff335042c3c52a6f60983f871dccb886c8cf3ca0844504a73db6.png)

  

We've drawn some rectangles to help us calculate our left Riemann sum, and we have chosen the heights of each rectangle to be calculated using the left endpoint of each interval. 

By calculating the area of each rectangle, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/29ee20f47383afc6f793767b4ad6bb7e12b81e2a5e911f27003f84504ecc05e1.svg)

Plugging our numbers into the above, we find

$$
\eqalign{
\mathcal{A}	&\approx	{\color{red}1} \cdot ({\color{blue}2-1})
						+ {\color{red}4} \cdot ({\color{blue}3.5-2})
						+ {\color{red}6} \cdot ({\color{blue}4-3.5}) \[5pt]
			&= {\color{red}1} \cdot {\color{blue}1} +{\color{red}4} \cdot {\color{blue}1.5}+ {\color{red}6} \cdot {\color{blue}0.5}  \[5pt]
			&=1+6+3\[5pt]
			&= 10.
}
$$

In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is computed as

$$
\mathcal{A}	\approx	f(0.0)\Delta x_1+f(0.8)\Delta x_2+f(1.6)\Delta x_3,
$$

where each $\Delta x_i$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
\Delta x_i = x_{i+1}-x_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $\Delta x$'s.

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.8$ | $1.6$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\Delta{x}$ | $0.8$ | $0.8$ | $0.4$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $2$ | $5$ | $10$ | $12$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈2\cdot 0.8+5\cdot 0.8+10\cdot 0.4 \\  & =1.6+4+4 \\  & =9.6.\end{aligned}
$$

 10pounds

 9pounds

In this case, we have n=3 rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

A≈w(0)Δt1+w(1)Δt2+w(3)Δt3,

where each Δti is calculated by considering the step between a particular t-value and the next one, i.e.,

Δti=ti+1−ti.

We set up a value table that includes the Δt's.

t 0 1 3 7
Δt 1 2 4 −
w(t) 1 2 1 3

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get A≈1⋅1+2⋅2+1⋅4=1+4+4=9.

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total weight lost by Daniel. He lost approximately 9 pounds.

Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/275b62fbec1c1a550cb23b481ec54c1e12d3d42e70cf95cd917f1b932638add4.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5))\cdot 0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)=4{x}^{2}-1$ at each left endpoint:

| $x$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $8$ | $15$ | $24$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3+8+15+24)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50\cdot 0.5 \\  & =25\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
A speedboat travels downstream on a river. The table below gives the speed $v(t)$, in miles per hour, of the boat at certain moments during its journey.

| $t\,(\text{hours})$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)\,(\text{mi/hour})$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ | $80$ |

Use a left Riemann sum for $v(t)$ over the interval $[0,2]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total distance traveled by the speedboat.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=2,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{2-0}{4}=0.5.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{v({x}_{0})+v({t}_{1})+…+v({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(v(0)+v(0.5)+v(1)+v(1.5))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $v(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v(t)$ | $10$ | $35$ | $40$ | $65$ |

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(10+35+40+65)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =150\cdot 0.5 \\  & =75\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance traveled by the speedboat. So, the distance is $75\,\text{mi}.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

A speedboat travels downstream on a river. The table below gives the speed v(t), in miles per hour, of the boat at certain moments during its journey.

t(hours) 0 0.5 1 1.5 2
v(t)(mi/hour) 10 35 40 65 80

Use a left Riemann sum for v(t) over the interval [0,2] with four subintervals to approximate the total distance traveled by the speedboat.

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.

a
 65mi
b
 115mi
c
 75mi
d
 110mi
e
 80mi
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's compute the step size Δt, which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are a=0 and b=2, and there are n=4 rectangles, so the step size is

Δt=b−an=2−04=0.5.

The area A can be approximated using the formula

A≈(v(x0)+v(t1)+…+v(tn−1)⏞heights)⋅Δt⏟ width=(v(0)+v(0.5)+v(1)+v(1.5))⋅Δt.

So, we now set up a table with the values of v(t) at each point:

t 0 0.5 1 1.5
v(t) 10 35 40 65

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area: A≈(10+35+40+65)⋅0.5=150⋅0.5=75

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance traveled by the speedboat. So, the distance is 75mi.

Question 2
?

A speedboat travels downstream on a river. The table below gives the speed v(t), in miles per hour, of the boat at certain moments during its journey.

t(hours) 0 0.5 1 1.5 2
v(t)(mi/hour) 10 35 40 65 80

Use a left Riemann sum for v(t) over the interval [0,2] with four subintervals to approximate the total distance traveled by the speedboat.

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.

a
 65mi
b
 115mi
c
 75mi
d
 110mi
e
 80mi
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's compute the step size Δt, which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are a=0 and b=2, and there are n=4 rectangles, so the step size is

Δt=b−an=2−04=0.5.

The area A can be approximated using the formula

A≈(v(x0)+v(t1)+…+v(tn−1)⏞heights)⋅Δt⏟ width=(v(0)+v(0.5)+v(1)+v(1.5))⋅Δt.

So, we now set up a table with the values of v(t) at each point:

t 0 0.5 1 1.5
v(t) 10 35 40 65

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area: A≈(10+35+40+65)⋅0.5=150⋅0.5=75

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total distance traveled by the speedboat. So, the distance is 75mi.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[1,10]$ with a regular step size. Estimate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[1,10]$ using a left Riemann sum with $3$ equal subintervals.

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ | $2$ |
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(1)+f(4)+f(7))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the interval $[1,10]$ is divided into $3$ equal subintervals, the width of each subinterval is

$$
Δx=\frac{10-1}{3}=3.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at the left endpoints:

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+0)\cdot 3 \\  & =3\cdot 3 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
A tank is filling with soda. The table below gives the rate $R(t)$, in liters per minute, at which the tank is filling at certain moments since it started.

| $t\,(\text{minutes})$ | $0$ | $3$ | $6$ | $9$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $R(t)\,(\text{liters/minute})$ | $30$ | $40$ | $60$ | $70$ | $90$ |

Given that the tank is empty when $t=0,$ use a left Riemann sum for $R(t)$ over the interval $[0,12]$ with four subintervals to approximate the total volume of soda in the tank after $12$ minutes.
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the step size $Δt,$ which is just the width of each rectangle. In this case, the endpoints of our interval are $a=0$ and $b=12,$ and there are $n=4$ rectangles, so the step size is

$$
Δt=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{12-0}{4}=3.
$$

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{R({t}_{0})+R({t}_{1})+…+R({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(R(0)+R(3)+R(6)+R(9))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $R(t)$ at each point:

t 0 3 6 9
R(t) 30 40 60 70

Now, we obtain the following approximation for the area: A≈(30+40+60+70)⋅3=200⋅3=600

question.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=3x-{x}^{2}$ over the interval $[0.5,2.5]$ using a left Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our situation.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/0e3f499cbc36c9dca7e759b67a8fd9e94959039f3403832e1d60b9ed598c44dd.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1.25$ | $2$ | $2.25$ | $2$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1.25+2+2.25+2)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =7.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =3.75\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Estimate the area under the curve y=3x−x2 over the interval [0.5,2.5] using a left Riemann sum with step size Δx=0.5.

a
7.53
b
5.35
c
3.75
d
7.35
e
3.57
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's sketch our situation.

The area A can be approximated using the formula

A≈(f(x0)+f(x1)+…+f(xn−1)⏞heights)⋅Δx⏟ width=(f(0.5)+f(1)+f(1.5)+f(2))⋅Δx.

So, we now set up a table with the values of f(x) at each point:

x 0.5 1 1.5 2
f(x) 1.25 2 2.25 2

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area: A≈(1.25+2+2.25+2)⋅0.5=7.5⋅0.5=3.75

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[-3,3]$ with a regular step size. If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $4$, then what must be the value of $k?$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $5$ |
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+…+f({x}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(-3)+f(-1)+f(1))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =(5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =10+2k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A$ must be $4$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}10+2k & =4 \\ 2k & =-6 \\ k & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

The table below gives the values of a continuous function f(x) over the closed interval [−3,3] with a regular step size. If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve y=f(x) with 3 subintervals defined by the given points has a value of 4, then what must be the value of k?

x −3 −1 1 3
f(x) 1 k 4 5
a
−3
b
−1
c
2
d
−2
e
1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area A can be approximated using the formula

A≈(f(x0)+f(x1)+…+f(xn−1)⏞heights)⋅Δx⏟ width=(f(−3)+f(−1)+f(1))⋅Δx.

So, we now set up a table with the values of f(x) at each point:

x −3 −1 1
f(x) 1 k 4

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

A≈(1+k+4)⋅2=(5+k)⋅2=10+2k

Finally, since we are given that A must be 4, we obtain 10+2k=42k=−6k=−3.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
The following table shows the rate of change of a city's temperature over a $10$-hour period, starting at $2\,\text{a.m}.$

| $t\,(\text{h})$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T\,{(}^{∘}\text{C}/\text{h})$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}$ has a value of $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ what is the value of $k?$
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ under the curve $y=T(t)$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{T({t}_{0})+T({t}_{1})+…+T({t}_{n-1})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δt}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(T(2)+T(4)+T(6)+T(8)+T(10))\cdot Δt.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $T(t)$ at each point:

| $t$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $T(t)$ | $1$ | $k$ | $4$ | $2$ | $3$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+k+4+2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =2(k+10) \\  & =2k+20\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total change in the temperature from $2\,\text{a.m}$ to $12\,\text{p.m}.$ Since we are given that the left Riemann sum approximation of the total change in the temperature is $26{\,}^{∘}\text{C},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2k+20 & =26 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the closed interval $[2,8]$ with a regular step size.

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ | $1$ |

If the left Riemann sum approximation of the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ with $3$ subintervals defined by the given points has a value of $18$, then what must be the value of $k?$ 

$\,\,k=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f({x}_{0})+f({x}_{1})+f({x}_{2})}})\cdot \,\,{{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{ }\text{width}} \\  & =(f(2)+f(4)+f(6))\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the points are $2,4,6,8$ with three subintervals, the step size is

$$
Δx=\frac{8-2}{3}=2.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each left-endpoint:

| $x$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-3$ | $5$ | $k$ |

So, we obtain the following approximation to the area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈((-3)+5+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =(2+k)\cdot 2 \\  & =4+2k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are given that $A=18$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}4+2k & =18 \\ 2k & =14 \\ k & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/671d5efc8abc559cf638bfbfdda76bddb0b8d5c2d9134dffbbf7eab0e2f0b25a.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $7$ | $17$ | $31$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+7+17+31)\cdot 1 \\  & =56\cdot 1 \\  & =56\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is strictly $\text{increasing}$ over the interval $[1,5],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an $\text{underestimate}$ of the actual area.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem: Estimate the area under the curve $y=-{x}^{2}+3x+1$ over the interval $[1.5,3.5]$ using a left Riemann sum with step size $Δx=0.5.$ Is this an overestimate or an underestimate?
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/ad1e85721eb2142f5cad422530aeed86c0919f34261d19e11e9f056cf355b387.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5)+f(3)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.25$ | $3$ | $2.25$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.25+3+2.25+1)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =9.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.75\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[1.5,3.5],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/ad1e85721eb2142f5cad422530aeed86c0919f34261d19e11e9f056cf355b387.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(1.5)+f(2)+f(2.5)+f(3)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $2.5$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3.25$ | $3$ | $2.25$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(3.25+3+2.25+1)\cdot 0.5 \\  & =9.5\cdot 0.5 \\  & =4.75\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is *strictly decreasing* over the interval $[1.5,3.5],$ the rectangles reach *above* the function, which means our approximation is an *overestimate* of the actual area.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14221930/assets/e8cd8966d69260c77685d349c97eceb1545686d347f6cdb827ad470880797bf5.png)

The area $A$ can be approximated using the formula

$$
A≈(\overset{\text{heights}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0)+f(0.25)+f(0.5)+f(0.75)}})\cdot {{Δx}_{⏟}}_{\text{width}}.
$$

So, we now set up a table with the values of $f(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $0$ | $0.25$ | $0.5$ | $0.75$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈(1+2+3+4)\cdot 0.25 \\  & =10\cdot 0.25 \\  & =2.5\end{aligned}
$$

Because the function is strictly $\text{increasing}$ over the interval $[0,1],$ the rectangles reach *below* the function, which means our approximation is an $\text{underestimate}$ of the actual area.

question.name: Question 16
question.problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[0,10].$

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $15$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[0,10].$
question.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(0)Δ{x}_{1}+f(3)Δ{x}_{2}+f(5)Δ{x}_{3}+f(7)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $3$ | $2$ | $2$ | $3$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $4$ | $5$ | $9$ | $15$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 3+4\cdot 2+5\cdot 2+9\cdot 3 \\  & =3+8+10+27 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.

$$

x 0 3 5 7 10
f(x) 1 4 5 9 15

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve y=f(x) over the interval [0,10].

a
48
b
45
c
39
d
56
e
52

EXPLANATION

In this case, we have n=4 rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

A≈f(0)Δx1+f(3)Δx2+f(5)Δx3+f(7)Δx4,

where each Δxi is calculated by considering the step between a particular x-value and the next one, i.e.,

Δxi=xi+1−xi.

We set up a value table that includes the Δx's.

x 0 3 5 7 10
Δx 3 2 2 3 −
f(x) 1 4 5 9 15

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get A≈1⋅3+4⋅2+5⋅2+9⋅3=3+8+10+27=48.

question.name: Question 17
question.problem:
Daniel decides to go on a diet. The table below gives the rate $w(t)$, in pounds per week, at which he loses weight over a period of $7$ weeks.

| $t\,(\text{week})$ | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $w(t)\,(\text{pounds/week})$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Use a left Riemann sum for $w(t)$ over the interval $[0,7]$ with three subintervals to approximate Daniel's total weight loss.
question.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈w(0)Δ{t}_{1}+w(1)Δ{t}_{2}+w(3)Δ{t}_{3},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i+1}-{t}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $-$ |
| $w(t)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 4 \\  & =1+4+4 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total weight lost by Daniel. He lost approximately $9$ pounds.

last_observation.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=3$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈w(0)Δ{t}_{1}+w(1)Δ{t}_{2}+w(3)Δ{t}_{3},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i+1}-{t}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $-$ |
| $w(t)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+1\cdot 4 \\  & =1+4+4 \\  & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, in the given context, the area under the curve represents the total weight lost by Daniel. He lost approximately $9$ pounds.

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ | $5$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $4$ | $6$ | $5$ | $9$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area $A$ under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[0,8].$ 

$A≈$

In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(0)Δ{x}_{1}+f(2)Δ{x}_{2}+f(5)Δ{x}_{3}+f(6)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ | $5$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $3$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $3$ | $4$ | $6$ | $5$ | $9$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈3\cdot 2+4\cdot 3+6\cdot 1+5\cdot 2 \\  & =6+12+6+10 \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
The following table shows the speed $v$, in $\text{km/min},$ at certain times during a family car trip over a period of $60$ minutes.

| $t\,(\text{min})$ | $60$ | $70$ | $80$ | $95$ | $110$ | $120$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $v\,(\text{km/min})$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1.5$ |

Assuming that the family traveled $130\,\text{km}$ during the first hour of the trip, use the left Riemann sum to approximate the total distance traveled during the first two hours.

*Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.*
question.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=5$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈v(60)Δ{t}_{1}+v(70)Δ{t}_{2}+v(80)Δ{t}_{3}+v(95)Δ{t}_{4}+v(110)Δ{t}_{5},
$$

where each $Δ{t}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $t$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{t}_{i}={t}_{i+1}-{t}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δt$'s.

| $t$ | $60$ | $70$ | $80$ | $95$ | $110$ | $120$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δt$ | $10$ | $10$ | $15$ | $15$ | $10$ | $-$ |
| $v(t)$ | $1.5$ | $2$ | $1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1.5$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈10\cdot 1.5+10\cdot 2+15\cdot 1+15\cdot 1+10\cdot 2 \\  & =15+20+15+15+20 \\  & =85\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the given context, the area under the curve represents the distance covered in $60$ minutes of travel, from $t=60$ minutes to $t=120$ minutes. The distance traveled in the first two hours is 

$$
\begin{aligned}d=130+85=215\,\text{km}.\end{aligned}
$$

The following table shows the speed v, in km/min, at certain times during a family car trip over a period of 60 minutes.

t(min) 60 70 80 95 110 120
v(km/min) 1.5 2 1 1 2 1.5

Assuming that the family traveled 130km during the first hour of the trip, use the left Riemann sum to approximate the total distance traveled during the first two hours.

Hint: The distance traveled is given by the area under the speed-time graph.

a
205km
b
215km
c
235km
d

In this case, we have n=5 rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

A≈v(60)Δt1+v(70)Δt2+v(80)Δt3+v(95)Δt4+v(110)Δt5,

where each Δti is calculated by considering the step between a particular t-value and the next one, i.e.,

Δti=ti+1−ti.

We set up a value table that includes the Δt's.

t 60 70 80 95 110 120
Δt 10 10 15 15 10 −
v(t) 1.5 2 1 1 2 1.5

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

A≈10⋅1.5+10⋅2+15⋅1+15⋅1+10⋅2=15+20+15+15+20=85km.

In the given context, the area under the curve represents the distance covered in 60 minutes of travel, from t=60 minutes to t=120 minutes. The distance traveled in the first two hours is

d=130+85=215km.

question.problem:
The following table shows some values of a continuous function $f(x)$ over the interval $[-3,5].$

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $3$ |

Use the left Riemann sum, with the four subintervals indicated by the data, to approximate the area under the curve $y=f(x)$ over the interval $[-3,5].$
question.worked_solution:
In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(-3)Δ{x}_{1}+f(-1)Δ{x}_{2}+f(0)Δ{x}_{3}+f(3)Δ{x}_{4},
$$

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$
Δ{x}_{i}={x}_{i+1}-{x}_{i}.
$$

We set up a value table that includes the $Δx$'s.

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $3$ | $5$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $Δx$ | $2$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $-$ |
| $f(x)$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $3$ |

Finally, we plug in the numbers to approximate the area under the curve and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈-1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 3+4\cdot 2 \\  & =-2+1+6+8 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we have $n=4$ rectangles. Using the left Riemann sum, the area is approximated as

$$
A≈f(-3)Δ{x}_{1}+f(-1)Δ{x}_{2}+f(0)Δ{x}_{3}+f(3)Δ{x}_{4},

where each $Δ{x}_{i}$ is calculated by considering the step between a particular $x$-value and the next one, i.e.,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈-1\cdot 2+1\cdot 1+2\cdot 3+4\cdot 2 \\  & =-2+1+6+8 \\  & =13.\end{aligned}
$$
